questions.question: Matrix [latex]P[/latex] is given as [latex]P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] The TRUE option is:

options.A: Trace of P is equal to the sum of the Eigen values of P.
options.D: Absolute magnitude of each Eigen value is 1.

questions.explanation: Given: [latex]P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Trace of P: [latex]\text{tr}(P) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3[/latex] Eigenvalues: Solve [latex]\det(P - \lambda I) = 0[/latex] [latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 0] - 0 + 1[0 - (1-\lambda)] = 0[/latex] [latex](1-\lambda)^3 - (1-\lambda) = 0[/latex] [latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1] = 0[/latex] [latex](1-\lambda)[\lambda^2 - 2\lambda] = 0[/latex] [latex](1-\lambda)\cdot\lambda(\lambda - 2) = 0[/latex] Eigenvalues: [latex]\lambda = 0, 1, 2[/latex] Sum of eigenvalues = [latex]0 + 1 + 2 = 3[/latex] = Trace Checking other options: (B) [latex]P^T P \neq I[/latex] (P is not orthogonal) (C) P is symmetric ([latex]P^T = P[/latex]), not skew-symmetric (D) Eigenvalues are 0, 1, 2  -  not all magnitude 1 Therefore, Option (A) is TRUE.
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Trace of P: [latex]\text{tr}(P) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3[/latex]

Eigenvalues: Solve [latex]\det(P - \lambda I) = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 0] - 0 + 1[0 - (1-\lambda)] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)^3 - (1-\lambda) = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[(1-\lambda)^2 - 1] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)[\lambda^2 - 2\lambda] = 0[/latex]
[latex](1-\lambda)\cdot\lambda(\lambda - 2) = 0[/latex]
Eigenvalues: [latex]\lambda = 0, 1, 2[/latex]

Sum of eigenvalues = [latex]0 + 1 + 2 = 3[/latex] = Trace

Checking other options:
(B) [latex]P^T P \neq I[/latex] (P is not orthogonal)
(C) P is symmetric ([latex]P^T = P[/latex]), not skew-symmetric
(D) Eigenvalues are 0, 1, 2 - not all magnitude 1

Therefore, Option (A) is TRUE.

questions.question: A thin-walled spherical gas balloon of radius [latex]R[/latex] and wall thickness [latex]t[/latex] ([latex]t \ll R[/latex]) is subjected to an internal (gauge) pressure [latex]p[/latex]. The maximum tensile and shear stresses in the balloon wall are, respectively:
questions.explanation: For a thin-walled sphere under internal pressure p: Step 1  -  Hoop stress (circumferential): By equilibrium: [latex]\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex] Both principal stresses are equal in magnitude (biaxial state). Step 2  -  Maximum shear stress: In-plane maximum shear stress: [latex]\tau_{max,in} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{pR}{2t} - \dfrac{pR}{2t}}{2} = 0[/latex] Since both principal stresses are equal, the in-plane shear stress is zero . Therefore: Maximum tensile stress = [latex]\dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex] Maximum shear stress = 0
questions.topic: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain
questions.explanation_html:
For a thin-walled sphere under internal pressure p:

Step 1 - Hoop stress (circumferential):
By equilibrium: [latex]\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex]

Both principal stresses are equal in magnitude (biaxial state).

Step 2 - Maximum shear stress:
In-plane maximum shear stress:
[latex]\tau_{max,in} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{pR}{2t} - \dfrac{pR}{2t}}{2} = 0[/latex]

Since both principal stresses are equal, the in-plane shear stress is zero.

Therefore:
Maximum tensile stress = [latex]\dfrac{pR}{2t}[/latex]
Maximum shear stress = 0

questions.question: Which one of the following is utilized to determine the long-term deformation of concrete under sustained loading?
questions.explanation: Definitions: Creep: Time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained (long-term) loading at constant stress. It is the phenomenon used to determine long-term deformation. Shrinkage: Volume change due to loss of moisture  -  not load-dependent. Modulus of Rupture: Flexural tensile strength of concrete  -  measured by beam bending test. Split Tensile Strength: Indirect tensile strength  -  measured by splitting a cylinder. Therefore, Creep is the property used to determine long-term deformation under sustained loading.
questions.explanation_html:
Definitions:

Creep: Time-dependent deformation of concrete under sustained (long-term) loading at constant stress. It is the phenomenon used to determine long-term deformation.

Shrinkage: Volume change due to loss of moisture - not load-dependent.

Modulus of Rupture: Flexural tensile strength of concrete - measured by beam bending test.

Split Tensile Strength: Indirect tensile strength - measured by splitting a cylinder.

Therefore, Creep is the property used to determine long-term deformation under sustained loading.

questions.question: Two reservoirs having different water levels are connected by two long parallel pipelines of same length and same material but having diameters of 600 mm and 400 mm. Using Darcy-Weisbach equation, the ratio of flowrate of water in the bigger diameter pipe to that in the smaller diameter pipe is
questions.explanation: Given: Two parallel pipes, same length L, same friction factor f, same head loss h. Diameters: [latex]D_1 = 600[/latex] mm, [latex]D_2 = 400[/latex] mm Darcy-Weisbach equation: [latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex] Since [latex]h_f[/latex], f, L are the same for both pipes: [latex]Q \propto D^{5/2}[/latex] Ratio of flowrates: [latex]\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{5/2} = \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{5/2} = (1.5)^{5/2}[/latex] [latex](1.5)^{5/2} = (1.5)^2 \times (1.5)^{0.5} = 2.25 \times 1.2247 = \mathbf{2.756} \approx \mathbf{2.76}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: Two parallel pipes, same length L, same friction factor f, same head loss h.
Diameters: [latex]D_1 = 600[/latex] mm, [latex]D_2 = 400[/latex] mm

Darcy-Weisbach equation:
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex]

Since [latex]h_f[/latex], f, L are the same for both pipes:
[latex]Q \propto D^{5/2}[/latex]

Ratio of flowrates:
[latex]\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2} = \left(\dfrac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{5/2} = \left(\dfrac{600}{400}\right)^{5/2} = (1.5)^{5/2}[/latex]

[latex](1.5)^{5/2} = (1.5)^2 \times (1.5)^{0.5} = 2.25 \times 1.2247 = \mathbf{2.756} \approx \mathbf{2.76}[/latex]

questions.question: An irrigation canal is to be designed to deliver 10 cumec to meet the peak demand of 7500 hectare of cropped area. The estimated canal losses are 50% of the head discharge. The duty (in hectare/cumec) on capacity of this canal is
questions.explanation: Step 1: Determine the relationship between head discharge and outlet discharge Let the head discharge (canal capacity) be [latex]Q_h[/latex] and the outlet delivery discharge be [latex]Q_o[/latex]. The canal losses are given as 50% of the head discharge: [latex]\text{Canal Losses} = 0.50\,Q_h[/latex] The outlet discharge is the head discharge minus the losses: [latex]Q_o = Q_h - \text{Canal Losses}[/latex] [latex]Q_o = Q_h - 0.50Q_h = 0.50Q_h[/latex] Step 2: Calculate the canal capacity The canal is required to deliver 10 cumec at the outlet. Therefore, [latex]10 = 0.50Q_h[/latex] [latex]Q_h = \frac{10}{0.50} = 20\ \text{cumec}[/latex] Thus, the head discharge (canal capacity) is: [latex]\boxed{Q_h = 20\ \text{cumec}}[/latex] Step 3: Compute the duty on canal capacity Duty on canal capacity is defined as the irrigated area per unit head discharge: [latex]D = \frac{\text{Area}}{Q_h}[/latex] Substituting the given values: [latex]D = \frac{7500}{20}[/latex] [latex]D = 375\ \text{hectare/cumec}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Determine the relationship between head discharge and outlet discharge

Let the head discharge (canal capacity) be [latex]Q_h[/latex] and the outlet delivery discharge be [latex]Q_o[/latex].

The canal losses are given as 50% of the head discharge:
[latex]\text{Canal Losses} = 0.50\,Q_h[/latex]

The outlet discharge is the head discharge minus the losses:
[latex]Q_o = Q_h - \text{Canal Losses}[/latex]
[latex]Q_o = Q_h - 0.50Q_h = 0.50Q_h[/latex]

Step 2: Calculate the canal capacity

The canal is required to deliver 10 cumec at the outlet. Therefore,
[latex]10 = 0.50Q_h[/latex]
[latex]Q_h = \frac{10}{0.50} = 20\ \text{cumec}[/latex]

Thus, the head discharge (canal capacity) is:
[latex]\boxed{Q_h = 20\ \text{cumec}}[/latex]

Step 3: Compute the duty on canal capacity

Duty on canal capacity is defined as the irrigated area per unit head discharge:
[latex]D = \frac{\text{Area}}{Q_h}[/latex]

Substituting the given values:
[latex]D = \frac{7500}{20}[/latex]
[latex]D = 375\ \text{hectare/cumec}[/latex]

questions.question: The Whole Circle Bearing (WCB) of line AB is [latex]150 ^\circ[/latex]. The length of AB is 100 m. The latitude and departure values, respectively, for this line are:
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Length of line AB, [latex]L = 100\ \text{m}[/latex]
Whole Circle Bearing (WCB) of AB, [latex]\theta = 150^\circ[/latex]

Step 1: Determine the quadrant

A WCB of [latex]150^\circ[/latex] lies between [latex]90^\circ[/latex] and [latex]180^\circ[/latex]. Therefore, the line lies in the South-East (SE) quadrant.

Hence:
Latitude = Negative (South)
Departure = Positive (East)

Step 2: Calculate Latitude

Latitude is given by:
[latex] \text{Latitude} = L\cos\theta = 100\cos 150^\circ =100(-0.8660) =-86.60\ \text{m} [/latex]

Step 3: Calculate Departure

Departure is given by:
[latex] \text{Departure} = L\sin\theta = 100\sin 150^\circ =100(0.5)=50.00\ \text{m} [/latex]

questions.question: The settling velocity of inorganic particles in the sedimentation tank of a water treatment plant is governed by
questions.explanation: Stokes' law gives the terminal settling velocity of a small spherical particle in a viscous fluid: [latex]v_s = \dfrac{(\rho_s - \rho_w) g d^2}{18\mu}[/latex] where: [latex]v_s[/latex] = settling velocity [latex]\rho_s[/latex] = density of particle [latex]\rho_w[/latex] = density of water [latex]g[/latex] = acceleration due to gravity [latex]d[/latex] = diameter of particle [latex]\mu[/latex] = dynamic viscosity of fluid Other laws: Darcy's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] groundwater flow through porous media Dupuit's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] unconfined aquifer flow assumption Bernoulli's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] energy conservation in flowing fluid Therefore, Settling velocity of inorganic particles is governed by Stokes' law .
questions.explanation_html:
Stokes' law gives the terminal settling velocity of a small spherical particle in a viscous fluid:

[latex]v_s = \dfrac{(\rho_s - \rho_w) g d^2}{18\mu}[/latex]

where:
[latex]v_s[/latex] = settling velocity
[latex]\rho_s[/latex] = density of particle
[latex]\rho_w[/latex] = density of water
[latex]g[/latex] = acceleration due to gravity
[latex]d[/latex] = diameter of particle
[latex]\mu[/latex] = dynamic viscosity of fluid

Other laws:
Darcy's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] groundwater flow through porous media
Dupuit's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] unconfined aquifer flow assumption
Bernoulli's law [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] energy conservation in flowing fluid

Therefore, Settling velocity of inorganic particles is governed by Stokes' law.

questions.question: Cant [latex]C[/latex] on a Broad Gauge railway track is calculated for an equilibrium speed [latex]V[/latex] (in km/h), dynamic gauge [latex]G[/latex] (in mm) and radius of curve [latex]R[/latex] (in m) using formula/formulae:
questions.explanation: Derivation of Cant formula: For a vehicle travelling at speed [latex]V[/latex] km/h on a curve of radius [latex]R[/latex] metres: Centrifugal acceleration [latex]= \dfrac{V^2}{R}[/latex] (in appropriate units) For equilibrium, the cant (superelevation) [latex]C[/latex] is: [latex] \dfrac{GV^2}{gR}[/latex] Converting V from km/h to m/s: [latex]V_{m/s} = \dfrac{V_{km/h}}{3.6}[/latex] [latex]C = \dfrac{G \cdot \left(\dfrac{V}{3.6}\right)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{9.81 \times 12.96 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127.1 R} \approx \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}[/latex] where G = dynamic gauge in mm, V in km/h, R in m. This is the standard Indian Railways formula for cant on Broad Gauge.
questions.explanation_html:
Derivation of Cant formula:

For a vehicle travelling at speed [latex]V[/latex] km/h on a curve of radius [latex]R[/latex] metres:

Centrifugal acceleration [latex]= \dfrac{V^2}{R}[/latex] (in appropriate units)

For equilibrium, the cant (superelevation) [latex]C[/latex] is: [latex] \dfrac{GV^2}{gR}[/latex]

Converting V from km/h to m/s: [latex]V_{m/s} = \dfrac{V_{km/h}}{3.6}[/latex]

[latex]C = \dfrac{G \cdot \left(\dfrac{V}{3.6}\right)^2}{9.81 \cdot R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{9.81 \times 12.96 \times R} = \dfrac{GV^2}{127.1 R} \approx \dfrac{GV^2}{127R}[/latex]

where G = dynamic gauge in mm, V in km/h, R in m.

This is the standard Indian Railways formula for cant on Broad Gauge.

questions.question: Which of the following components is/are NOT removed in the secondary treatment of sewage?
questions.explanation: (A) Suspended settleable organic solids These are removed mainly in primary sedimentation tanks, not in secondary treatment. Therefore, they are not removed in secondary treatment. (B) Colloids including dissolved organic matter This is the main target of secondary treatment. Hence, removed. (C) Pathogens Secondary treatment may reduce pathogens but does not reliably remove them. Disinfection is required for pathogen removal. Hence, not removed. (D) Fat and grease These are primarily removed during preliminary/primary treatment by skimming. Hence, not removed in secondary treatment.
questions.explanation_html:
(A) Suspended settleable organic solids
These are removed mainly in primary sedimentation tanks, not in secondary treatment. Therefore, they are not removed in secondary treatment.

(B) Colloids including dissolved organic matter
This is the main target of secondary treatment. Hence, removed.

(C) Pathogens
Secondary treatment may reduce pathogens but does not reliably remove them. Disinfection is required for pathogen removal. Hence, not removed.

(D) Fat and grease
These are primarily removed during preliminary/primary treatment by skimming. Hence, not removed in secondary treatment.

questions.question: Bag I contains 4 white and 6 black balls. Bag II contains 4 white and 3 black balls. One ball is drawn at random from any one of the two bags and it is found to be a black ball. The probability that the black ball was drawn from Bag I is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: Bag I: 4 white + 6 black = 10 balls Bag II: 4 white + 3 black = 7 balls Using Bayes' Theorem: Let B = event of drawing a black ball Let [latex]B_1[/latex] = Bag I chosen, [latex]B_2[/latex] = Bag II chosen [latex]P(B_1) = P(B_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex] (equal probability of choosing either bag) [latex]P(B | B_1) = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6[/latex] [latex]P(B | B_2) = \dfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.4286[/latex] Total probability of black ball: [latex]P(B) = P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1) + P(B_2) \cdot P(B|B_2)[/latex] [latex]P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{14} = \dfrac{21}{70} + \dfrac{15}{70} = \dfrac{36}{70}[/latex] Probability black ball came from Bag I: [latex]P(B_1|B) = \dfrac{P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{70}{36} = \dfrac{210}{360} = \dfrac{7}{12} \approx \mathbf{0.58}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Bag I: 4 white + 6 black = 10 balls
Bag II: 4 white + 3 black = 7 balls

Using Bayes' Theorem:
Let B = event of drawing a black ball
Let [latex]B_1[/latex] = Bag I chosen, [latex]B_2[/latex] = Bag II chosen

[latex]P(B_1) = P(B_2) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex] (equal probability of choosing either bag)

[latex]P(B | B_1) = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6[/latex]
[latex]P(B | B_2) = \dfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.4286[/latex]

Total probability of black ball:
[latex]P(B) = P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1) + P(B_2) \cdot P(B|B_2)[/latex]
[latex]P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10} + \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{3}{14} = \dfrac{21}{70} + \dfrac{15}{70} = \dfrac{36}{70}[/latex]

Probability black ball came from Bag I:
[latex]P(B_1|B) = \dfrac{P(B_1) \cdot P(B|B_1)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{6}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3}{10}}{\dfrac{36}{70}} = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{70}{36} = \dfrac{210}{360} = \dfrac{7}{12} \approx \mathbf{0.58}[/latex]

questions.question: A matrix is given as: [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] By performing Cholesky decomposition, [latex]|l_{22}|[/latex] of the lower triangular matrix is ______ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Given matrix: [latex]A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Cholesky decomposition: [latex]A = LL^T[/latex], where [latex]L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Step 1  -  Find [latex]l_{11}[/latex]: [latex]l_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} = \sqrt{9} = 3[/latex] Step 2  -  Find [latex]l_{21}[/latex]: [latex]l_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{l_{11}} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5[/latex] Step 3  -  Find [latex]l_{22}[/latex]: [latex]l_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - l_{21}^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5[/latex] [latex]|l_{22}| = \mathbf{5}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given matrix: [latex]A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 15 \\ 15 & 50 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Cholesky decomposition: [latex]A = LL^T[/latex], where [latex]L = \begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 \\ l_{21} & l_{22} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

Step 1 - Find [latex]l_{11}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{11} = \sqrt{a_{11}} = \sqrt{9} = 3[/latex]

Step 2 - Find [latex]l_{21}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{21} = \dfrac{a_{21}}{l_{11}} = \dfrac{15}{3} = 5[/latex]

Step 3 - Find [latex]l_{22}[/latex]:
[latex]l_{22} = \sqrt{a_{22} - l_{21}^2} = \sqrt{50 - 25} = \sqrt{25} = 5[/latex]

[latex]|l_{22}| = \mathbf{5}[/latex]

questions.question: It is given that [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] are integers in the following equation: [latex](x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0[/latex] The value of [latex](x^3 + y^3)[/latex] is ________ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Given: [latex](x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0[/latex] Key insight: Sum of two squares equals zero only when each square is zero . [latex](x + y - 7)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 7 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex] [latex](y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow y + 3x = 13 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex] Solving the system: Subtract (1) from (2): [latex](y + 3x) - (x + y) = 13 - 7[/latex] [latex]2x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 3[/latex] Substitute into (1): [latex]3 + y = 7 \Rightarrow y = 4[/latex] Calculate [latex]x^3 + y^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 = 27 + 64 = \mathbf{91}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex](x + y - 7)^2 + (y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0[/latex]

Key insight: Sum of two squares equals zero only when each square is zero.

[latex](x + y - 7)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow x + y = 7 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]
[latex](y + 3x - 13)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow y + 3x = 13 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Solving the system:
Subtract (1) from (2):
[latex](y + 3x) - (x + y) = 13 - 7[/latex]
[latex]2x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 3[/latex]

Substitute into (1): [latex]3 + y = 7 \Rightarrow y = 4[/latex]

Calculate [latex]x^3 + y^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 = 27 + 64 = \mathbf{91}[/latex]

questions.question: The required centre-to-centre spacing of 10 mm diameter bars is 150 mm to resist the design moment in a concrete slab. Instead of 10 mm diameter bars, if 12 mm diameter bars of the same grade are used, the required centre-to-centre spacing (in mm) to resist the same design moment becomes ________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Concept: The area of steel per unit width must remain the same to resist the same design moment. Given: 10 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_1 = 150[/latex] mm 12 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_2 = ?[/latex] Area of steel per unit width must be equal: [latex]\dfrac{A_{st1}}{s_1} = \dfrac{A_{st2}}{s_2}[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{\pi/4 \times 10^2}{150} = \dfrac{\pi/4 \times 12^2}{s_2}[/latex] [latex]s_2 = 150 \times \dfrac{12^2}{10^2} = 150 \times \dfrac{144}{100} = 150 \times 1.44 = \mathbf{216 \text{ mm}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Concept: The area of steel per unit width must remain the same to resist the same design moment.

Given:
10 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_1 = 150[/latex] mm
12 mm bars at spacing [latex]s_2 = ?[/latex]

Area of steel per unit width must be equal:
[latex]\dfrac{A_{st1}}{s_1} = \dfrac{A_{st2}}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac{\pi/4 \times 10^2}{150} = \dfrac{\pi/4 \times 12^2}{s_2}[/latex]

[latex]s_2 = 150 \times \dfrac{12^2}{10^2} = 150 \times \dfrac{144}{100} = 150 \times 1.44 = \mathbf{216 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

questions.question: Two steel plates are to be connected together by a 5 mm fillet weld of length 150 mm to transfer a design load. If the size of the fillet weld used to connect the same two plates is changed to 6 mm, the weld length (in mm) needed for transferring the same design load is ________ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Concept: The design strength of a fillet weld = weld size x throat factor x length x weld strength. For the same load, the product (size x length) must remain constant. Given: Original: size [latex]s_1 = 5[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_1 = 150[/latex] mm New: size [latex]s_2 = 6[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_2 = ?[/latex] Equating weld capacity: [latex]s_1 \times L_1 = s_2 \times L_2[/latex] [latex]5 \times 150 = 6 \times L_2[/latex] [latex]L_2 = \dfrac{750}{6} = \mathbf{125 \text{ mm}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Concept: The design strength of a fillet weld = weld size x throat factor x length x weld strength.
For the same load, the product (size x length) must remain constant.

Given:
Original: size [latex]s_1 = 5[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_1 = 150[/latex] mm
New: size [latex]s_2 = 6[/latex] mm, length [latex]L_2 = ?[/latex]

Equating weld capacity:
[latex]s_1 \times L_1 = s_2 \times L_2[/latex]
[latex]5 \times 150 = 6 \times L_2[/latex]
[latex]L_2 = \dfrac{750}{6} = \mathbf{125 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

questions.question: For a liquid, the permeability of a sandy soil having a void ratio of 0.60 was determined as 0.14 cm/s. Considering the same liquid and by using Taylor's equation, the permeability (in cm/s) of this soil corresponding to the void ratio of 0.80 is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Permeability corresponding to void ratio [latex]e_1=0.60[/latex] is [latex] k_1=0.14\ \text{cm/s} [/latex]

The required void ratio is [latex] e_2=0.80 [/latex]

Using Taylor's equation for permeability: [latex] k \propto \dfrac{e^3}{1+e} [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \frac{\dfrac{e_2^3}{1+e_2}} {\dfrac{e_1^3}{1+e_1}} [/latex]

Substituting the given values:
[latex] \begin{aligned} k_2 &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{(0.80)^3}{1+0.80}} {\dfrac{(0.60)^3}{1+0.60}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{0.512}{1.8}} {\dfrac{0.216}{1.6}}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14\left(\dfrac{0.2844}{0.135}\right)\\[4pt] &=0.14(2.107)\\ &=0.295 \end{aligned} [/latex]

questions.question: To obtain undisturbed clay soil sample, an Area Ratio of 10% needs to be achieved for a thin walled sampling tube. If the outer diameter of the tube is 50.8 mm, the inner diameter (in mm) is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Area Ratio formula: [latex]A_r = \dfrac{D_e^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2} \times 100\%[/latex] Given, [latex]A_r = 10\%[/latex], [latex]D_e = 50.8[/latex] mm, Solving for [latex]D_i[/latex] [latex]0.10 = \dfrac{50.8^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2}[/latex] [latex]0.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 - D_i^2[/latex] [latex]1.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 = 2580.64[/latex] [latex]D_i^2 = \dfrac{2580.64}{1.10} = 2346.04[/latex] [latex]D_i = \sqrt{2346.04} = \mathbf{48.4 \text{ mm}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Area Ratio formula:
[latex]A_r = \dfrac{D_e^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2} \times 100\%[/latex]

Given, [latex]A_r = 10\%[/latex], [latex]D_e = 50.8[/latex] mm, Solving for [latex]D_i[/latex]

[latex]0.10 = \dfrac{50.8^2 - D_i^2}{D_i^2}[/latex]

[latex]0.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 - D_i^2[/latex]

[latex]1.10 \cdot D_i^2 = 50.8^2 = 2580.64[/latex]

[latex]D_i^2 = \dfrac{2580.64}{1.10} = 2346.04[/latex]

[latex]D_i = \sqrt{2346.04} = \mathbf{48.4 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

questions.question: The travel times of three vehicles on a 2 km stretch of road are 4, 5, and 8 minutes. Assuming the speed of each vehicle to be constant in this stretch, the Space Mean Speed (in km/h) of the vehicles is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Space Mean Speed (SMS) is the harmonic mean of individual speeds. Given: Distance = 2 km, Travel times = 4, 5, 8 minutes Step 1  -  Individual speeds: [latex]v_1 = \dfrac{2 \text{ km}}{4/60 \text{ h}} = 30 \text{ km/h}[/latex] [latex]v_2 = \dfrac{2}{5/60} = 24 \text{ km/h}[/latex] [latex]v_3 = \dfrac{2}{8/60} = 15 \text{ km/h}[/latex] Step 2  -  Space Mean Speed (harmonic mean): [latex]SMS = \dfrac{n}{\sum \dfrac{1}{v_i}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{15}}[/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{4}{120} + \dfrac{5}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{17}{120}} = \dfrac{3 \times 120}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} = \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex] Alternatively: [latex]SMS = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Average travel time}} = \dfrac{2}{(4+5+8)/(3 \times 60)} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 \times 60}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} \approx \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Space Mean Speed (SMS) is the harmonic mean of individual speeds.

Given: Distance = 2 km, Travel times = 4, 5, 8 minutes

Step 1 - Individual speeds:
[latex]v_1 = \dfrac{2 \text{ km}}{4/60 \text{ h}} = 30 \text{ km/h}[/latex]
[latex]v_2 = \dfrac{2}{5/60} = 24 \text{ km/h}[/latex]
[latex]v_3 = \dfrac{2}{8/60} = 15 \text{ km/h}[/latex]

Step 2 - Space Mean Speed (harmonic mean):
[latex]SMS = \dfrac{n}{\sum \dfrac{1}{v_i}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{1}{30} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \dfrac{1}{15}}[/latex]

[latex]= \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{4}{120} + \dfrac{5}{120} + \dfrac{8}{120}} = \dfrac{3}{\dfrac{17}{120}} = \dfrac{3 \times 120}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} = \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex]

Alternatively: [latex]SMS = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Average travel time}} = \dfrac{2}{(4+5+8)/(3 \times 60)} = \dfrac{2 \times 3 \times 60}{17} = \dfrac{360}{17} \approx \mathbf{21.18 \text{ km/h}}[/latex]

questions.question: A 30 m long tape is standardized at [latex]25 ^\circ C[/latex]. It was used to measure the length of a line which came out to be 200 m. The temperature during the measurement was [latex]35 ^\circ C[/latex]. The coefficient of expansion of the tape was [latex]11 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ C[/latex]. The correction in the measured length (in mm) due to change in temperature is ______ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Correction due to temperature change: [latex]C_T = \alpha \cdot (T_m - T_s) \cdot L[/latex] Given: [latex]\alpha = 11 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ C[/latex] [latex]T_m = 35 ^\circ C[/latex] (measurement temperature) [latex]T_s = 25^\circ C[/latex] (standard temperature) [latex]L = 200[/latex] m (measured length) Calculation: [latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times (35 - 25) \times 200[/latex] [latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 10 \times 200[/latex] [latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 2000[/latex] [latex]C_T = 0.022 \text{ m} = \mathbf{22 \text{ mm}}[/latex] Note: Since temperature increased, the tape expanded, so the actual length is slightly more than measured. The correction is positive (+22 mm).
questions.explanation_html:
Correction due to temperature change:
[latex]C_T = \alpha \cdot (T_m - T_s) \cdot L[/latex]

Given:
[latex]\alpha = 11 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ C[/latex]
[latex]T_m = 35 ^\circ C[/latex] (measurement temperature)
[latex]T_s = 25^\circ C[/latex] (standard temperature)
[latex]L = 200[/latex] m (measured length)

Calculation:
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times (35 - 25) \times 200[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 10 \times 200[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 11 \times 10^{-6} \times 2000[/latex]
[latex]C_T = 0.022 \text{ m} = \mathbf{22 \text{ mm}}[/latex]

Note: Since temperature increased, the tape expanded, so the actual length is slightly more than measured. The correction is positive (+22 mm).

questions.question: The height of the plane of collimation of a levelling instrument is 100.000 m from a datum. The levelling instrument measures a Back Sight of 1.500 m on a vertically held staff at a ground point P. The reduced level (in m) of the ground point P with respect to the datum is ______ (rounded off to three decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: Height of Plane of Collimation (HPC) = 100.000 m Back Sight (BS) on staff at point P = 1.500 m Concept: [latex]\text{HPC} = \text{RL of P} + \text{BS}[/latex] Therefore: [latex]\text{RL of P} = \text{HPC} - \text{BS}[/latex] [latex]\text{RL of P} = 100.000 - 1.500 = \mathbf{98.500 \text{ m}}[/latex] Explanation: The staff reading (back sight) is taken at a known/benchmark point. The HPC is height of the instrument line of sight. The RL of P is obtained by subtracting the staff reading from the HPC.
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Height of Plane of Collimation (HPC) = 100.000 m
Back Sight (BS) on staff at point P = 1.500 m

Concept:
[latex]\text{HPC} = \text{RL of P} + \text{BS}[/latex]

Therefore:
[latex]\text{RL of P} = \text{HPC} - \text{BS}[/latex]
[latex]\text{RL of P} = 100.000 - 1.500 = \mathbf{98.500 \text{ m}}[/latex]

Explanation: The staff reading (back sight) is taken at a known/benchmark point. The HPC is height of the instrument line of sight. The RL of P is obtained by subtracting the staff reading from the HPC.

questions.question: Let [latex]f(x)[/latex] be a continuous function defined in [latex][0,2] \to \mathbb{R}[/latex] and satisfying the equation: [latex]\int_0^2 f(x)[x - f(x)]\, dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] The value of [latex]f(1)[/latex] is:
questions.explanation: Given: [latex]\int_0^2 f(x)[x - f(x)]\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] Expand the integrand: [latex]\int_0^2 x \cdot f(x)\,dx - \int_0^2 [f(x)]^2\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] Rearrange using completing the square: [latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] Evaluate [latex]\int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx[/latex]: [latex]= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{x^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] Substituting: [latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex] [latex]\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx = 0[/latex] Since the integrand is non-negative and continuous: [latex]f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2} \text{ for all } x \in [0, 2][/latex] [latex]f(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]\int_0^2 f(x)[x - f(x)]\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Expand the integrand:
[latex]\int_0^2 x \cdot f(x)\,dx - \int_0^2 [f(x)]^2\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Rearrange using completing the square:
[latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Evaluate [latex]\int_0^2 \dfrac{x^2}{4}\,dx[/latex]:
[latex]= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{x^3}{3}\Big|_0^2 = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]

Substituting:
[latex]-\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}[/latex]
[latex]\int_0^2 \left[f(x) - \dfrac{x}{2}\right]^2 dx = 0[/latex]

Since the integrand is non-negative and continuous:
[latex]f(x) = \dfrac{x}{2} \text{ for all } x \in [0, 2][/latex]

[latex]f(1) = \dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

questions.question: An ordinary differential equation is given below: [latex]x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y[/latex] Considering [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] as arbitrary constants, the general solution of the equation is
questions.explanation: Given ODE: [latex]x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]x^2 y'' - 6y = 0[/latex] This is an Euler-Cauchy equation . Assume [latex]y = x^m[/latex]: [latex]y' = mx^{m-1},\quad y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}[/latex] Substituting: [latex]x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} - 6x^m = 0[/latex] [latex]m(m-1)x^m - 6x^m = 0[/latex] [latex][m(m-1) - 6]x^m = 0[/latex] [latex]m^2 - m - 6 = 0[/latex] [latex](m-3)(m+2) = 0[/latex] [latex]m = 3 \text{ or } m = -2[/latex] General solution: [latex]y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given ODE: [latex]x^2 \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 6y[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]x^2 y'' - 6y = 0[/latex]

This is an Euler-Cauchy equation. Assume [latex]y = x^m[/latex]:

[latex]y' = mx^{m-1},\quad y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}[/latex]

Substituting:
[latex]x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} - 6x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex]m(m-1)x^m - 6x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex][m(m-1) - 6]x^m = 0[/latex]
[latex]m^2 - m - 6 = 0[/latex]
[latex](m-3)(m+2) = 0[/latex]
[latex]m = 3 \text{ or } m = -2[/latex]

General solution:
[latex]y(x) = ax^3 + bx^{-2} = ax^3 + \dfrac{b}{x^2}[/latex]

questions.question: A plane truss consists of two linearly elastic, homogeneous, identical members, namely PQ and QR. Both members have length [latex]L[/latex], cross-sectional area [latex]A[/latex], and modulus of elasticity [latex]E[/latex]. The members are inclined at [latex]45 ^\circ [/latex] as shown in the figure. The truss has hinge supports at P and R. The translational degrees-of-freedom ([latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex]) are shown at joint Q. After application of the boundary conditions, the stiffness matrix of the truss becomes:
questions.explanation: Setup: Members PQ and QR, each inclined at 45[latex]^\circ [/latex], hinge supports at P and R, free DOFs at Q: u (horizontal) and v (vertical). questions.question: Locations P and Q are separated by a wide valley. The difference in levels of locations P and Q measured by a levelling instrument stationed near P is 3.0 m. The same instrument stationed near Q measures the difference in levels of locations P and Q as -1.0 m. Assume that the atmospheric refraction is same during the measurements. The true difference in levels (in m) of locations P and Q is
questions.explanation:
Given: Difference in levels measured with the instrument near P: 
[latex]
h_1 = 3.0\ \text{m}
[/latex]

Difference in levels measured with the instrument near Q: 
[latex]
h_2 = -1.0\ \text{m}
[/latex] Because the stations are separated by a wide valley, the observations are affected by the combined error due to curvature and refraction. Let this error be [latex]e[/latex]. When the instrument is near P: 
[latex]
h_1 = H + e
[/latex] When the instrument is near Q: 
[latex]
h_2 = H - e
[/latex] where [latex]H[/latex] is the true difference in levels. Adding the two equations: [latex]
\begin{aligned}
h_1+h_2
&=(H+e)+(H-e)\\
&=2H
\end{aligned}
[/latex] Therefore, [latex]
\begin{aligned}
H
&=\frac{h_1+h_2}{2}\\
&=\frac{3.0+(-1.0)}{2}\\
&=\frac{2.0}{2}\\
&=1.0\ \text{m}
\end{aligned}
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Difference in levels measured with the instrument near P: [latex] h_1 = 3.0\ \text{m} [/latex] Difference in levels measured with the instrument near Q: [latex] h_2 = -1.0\ \text{m} [/latex]

Because the stations are separated by a wide valley, the observations are affected by the combined error due to curvature and refraction. Let this error be [latex]e[/latex].

When the instrument is near P: [latex] h_1 = H + e [/latex]
When the instrument is near Q: [latex] h_2 = H - e [/latex]
where [latex]H[/latex] is the true difference in levels.

Adding the two equations:
[latex] \begin{aligned} h_1+h_2 &=(H+e)+(H-e)\\ &=2H \end{aligned} [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] \begin{aligned} H &=\frac{h_1+h_2}{2}\\ &=\frac{3.0+(-1.0)}{2}\\ &=\frac{2.0}{2}\\ &=1.0\ \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

questions.question: As per Rankine's earth pressure theory, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

options.A: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ+ \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.B: For active earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.C: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ + \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.
options.D: For passive earth pressure, inclination of failure plane is [latex](45^\circ - \phi/2)[/latex] w.r.t. major principal plane.

questions.explanation_html:
Key Concept:

According to Rankine's earth pressure theory, the failure plane is inclined at
[latex] \boxed{45^\circ+\frac{\phi}{2}} [/latex] with respect to the major principal plane.

Active Earth Pressure Condition

In the active state, the vertical stress is the major principal stress. Therefore, the failure plane makes an angle of
[latex] 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} [/latex] with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (A) is True
Option (B) is False

Passive Earth Pressure Condition

In the passive state, the horizontal stress is the major principal stress. The failure plane still makes an angle of
[latex] 45^\circ+\dfrac{\phi}{2} [/latex] with the major principal plane.

Hence:
Option (C) is True
Option (D) is False

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE in the context of the geometric design of highways?

options.A:
The coefficient of friction used for the design of horizontal curves is lower than the 
coefficient of friction used in the computation of the sight distances.
options.B:
Centrifugal force at horizontal curve is counteracted by raising the middle of the 
pavement with respect to the edges.
options.C: Grade compensation is achieved by increasing the gradient of the horizontal curve.
options.D:
Under identical conditions, the design length of the summit curve of a road having 
unidirectional flow will be greater than that of the same road having bidirectional 
flow.

questions.explanation: (A) TRUE: Coefficient of friction for horizontal curve design (f = 0.10-0.15) is indeed lower than that used for sight distance/braking (f = 0.35-0.40). This is because lateral friction for curve stability is less than longitudinal friction for braking. (B) FALSE: Centrifugal force is counteracted by raising the outer edge of the pavement (superelevation/cant), not the middle. (C) FALSE: Grade compensation means reducing (not increasing) the gradient on horizontal curves to compensate for the extra resistance due to curvature. (D) FALSE: For unidirectional flow, the stopping sight distance (SSD) is used, which is shorter than the overtaking sight distance (OSD) used for bidirectional flow. Summit curve length [latex]\propto[/latex] SSD² or OSD². Since OSD > SSD, bidirectional needs longer curve. So unidirectional summit curve is shorter , not longer.

(A) TRUE: Coefficient of friction for horizontal curve design (f = 0.10-0.15) is indeed lower than that used for sight distance/braking (f = 0.35-0.40). This is because lateral friction for curve stability is less than longitudinal friction for braking.

(B) FALSE: Centrifugal force is counteracted by raising the outer edge of the pavement (superelevation/cant), not the middle.

(C) FALSE: Grade compensation means reducing (not increasing) the gradient on horizontal curves to compensate for the extra resistance due to curvature.

(D) FALSE: For unidirectional flow, the stopping sight distance (SSD) is used, which is shorter than the overtaking sight distance (OSD) used for bidirectional flow. Summit curve length [latex]\propto[/latex] SSD² or OSD². Since OSD > SSD, bidirectional needs longer curve. So unidirectional summit curve is shorter, not longer.

questions.question: Starting with the first approximation as [latex]x = 0.5[/latex], the second approximation for the root of the following function by the Newton-Raphson method is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places). [latex]f(x) = e^{-x} - x[/latex]
questions.explanation: Given: [latex]f(x) = e^{-x} - x[/latex], first approximation [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex] Newton-Raphson formula: [latex]x_1 = x_0 - \dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}[/latex] Step 1  -  Compute [latex]f'(x)[/latex]: [latex]f'(x) = -e^{-x} - 1[/latex] Step 2  -  Evaluate at [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex]: [latex]f(0.5) = e^{-0.5} - 0.5 = 0.6065 - 0.5 = 0.1065[/latex] [latex]f'(0.5) = -e^{-0.5} - 1 = -0.6065 - 1 = -1.6065[/latex] Step 3  -  Second approximation: [latex]x_1 = 0.5 - \dfrac{0.1065}{-1.6065} = 0.5 + 0.0663 = \mathbf{0.57}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]f(x) = e^{-x} - x[/latex], first approximation [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex]

Newton-Raphson formula:
[latex]x_1 = x_0 - \dfrac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}[/latex]

Step 1 - Compute [latex]f'(x)[/latex]:
[latex]f'(x) = -e^{-x} - 1[/latex]

Step 2 - Evaluate at [latex]x_0 = 0.5[/latex]:
[latex]f(0.5) = e^{-0.5} - 0.5 = 0.6065 - 0.5 = 0.1065[/latex]
[latex]f'(0.5) = -e^{-0.5} - 1 = -0.6065 - 1 = -1.6065[/latex]

Step 3 - Second approximation:
[latex]x_1 = 0.5 - \dfrac{0.1065}{-1.6065} = 0.5 + 0.0663 = \mathbf{0.57}[/latex]

questions.question:
Values of [latex]y[/latex] for different values of [latex]x[/latex] are tabulated below: [latex]
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
x & -2 & 1 & 2 \\
\hline
y & 28 & 4 & 16 \\
\hline
\end{array}
[/latex] If a second-degree interpolating polynomial [latex]P_2(x)[/latex] is used to represent [latex]y[/latex], the value of [latex]P_2(0)[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Given data points: (-2, 28), (1, 4), (2, 16) Using Lagrange's interpolation formula: [latex]P_2(x) = y_0 \cdot L_0(x) + y_1 \cdot L_1(x) + y_2 \cdot L_2(x)[/latex] [latex]L_0(x) = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-2-1)(-2-2)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-3)(-4)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{12}[/latex] [latex]L_1(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(1+2)(1-2)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(3)(-1)} = \dfrac{(x^2-4)}{-3}[/latex] [latex]L_2(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{(2+2)(2-1)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{4}[/latex] At x = 0: [latex]L_0(0) = \dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{12} = \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{6}[/latex] [latex]L_1(0) = \dfrac{(0-4)}{-3} = \dfrac{4}{3}[/latex] [latex]L_2(0) = \dfrac{(2)(-1)}{4} = \dfrac{-2}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{2}[/latex] [latex]P_2(0) = 28 \times \dfrac{1}{6} + 4 \times \dfrac{4}{3} + 16 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)[/latex] [latex]= \dfrac{28}{6} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{14}{3} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{30}{3} - 8 = 10 - 8 = \mathbf{2}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given data points: (-2, 28), (1, 4), (2, 16)

Using Lagrange's interpolation formula:
[latex]P_2(x) = y_0 \cdot L_0(x) + y_1 \cdot L_1(x) + y_2 \cdot L_2(x)[/latex]

[latex]L_0(x) = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-2-1)(-2-2)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{(-3)(-4)} = \dfrac{(x-1)(x-2)}{12}[/latex]

[latex]L_1(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(1+2)(1-2)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-2)}{(3)(-1)} = \dfrac{(x^2-4)}{-3}[/latex]

[latex]L_2(x) = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{(2+2)(2-1)} = \dfrac{(x+2)(x-1)}{4}[/latex]

At x = 0:
[latex]L_0(0) = \dfrac{(-1)(-2)}{12} = \dfrac{2}{12} = \dfrac{1}{6}[/latex]
[latex]L_1(0) = \dfrac{(0-4)}{-3} = \dfrac{4}{3}[/latex]
[latex]L_2(0) = \dfrac{(2)(-1)}{4} = \dfrac{-2}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{2}[/latex]

[latex]P_2(0) = 28 \times \dfrac{1}{6} + 4 \times \dfrac{4}{3} + 16 \times \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)[/latex]
[latex]= \dfrac{28}{6} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{14}{3} + \dfrac{16}{3} - 8 = \dfrac{30}{3} - 8 = 10 - 8 = \mathbf{2}[/latex]

questions.question: Two identical blocks A and B are connected by a rigid rod. The blocks rest against vertical and horizontal planes, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction at the vertical and horizontal planes is the same. If the sliding impends when [latex]\theta = 45^\circ [/latex], the value of the coefficient of static friction is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Setup: Blocks A (on vertical wall) and B (on horizontal floor), connected by rigid rod at angle [latex]\theta = 45^\circ [/latex]. Same coefficient of friction [latex]\mu[/latex] at both surfaces. Sliding impends. Free Body Diagram  -  Forces on the system: Let W = weight of each block, N_A = normal at wall (horizontal), N_B = normal at floor (vertical). Friction at wall: [latex]F_A = \mu N_A[/latex] (upward, opposing downward sliding) Friction at floor: [latex]F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] (opposing motion) Equilibrium equations: Horizontal: [latex]N_A = F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_A = \mu N_B \quad (1)[/latex] Vertical: [latex]N_B + F_A = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B + \mu N_A = 2W \quad (2)[/latex] From (1) into (2): [latex]N_B + \mu^2 N_B = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B(1 + \mu^2) = 2W[/latex] Moment about contact point using rod geometry at [latex]\theta = 45^\circ[/latex]: [latex]\mu = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \tan(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{0.41}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Setup: Blocks A (on vertical wall) and B (on horizontal floor), connected by rigid rod at angle [latex]\theta = 45^\circ [/latex]. Same coefficient of friction [latex]\mu[/latex] at both surfaces. Sliding impends.

Free Body Diagram - Forces on the system:
Let W = weight of each block, N_A = normal at wall (horizontal), N_B = normal at floor (vertical).

Friction at wall: [latex]F_A = \mu N_A[/latex] (upward, opposing downward sliding)
Friction at floor: [latex]F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] (opposing motion)

Equilibrium equations:
Horizontal: [latex]N_A = F_B = \mu N_B[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_A = \mu N_B \quad (1)[/latex]
Vertical: [latex]N_B + F_A = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B + \mu N_A = 2W \quad (2)[/latex]

From (1) into (2): [latex]N_B + \mu^2 N_B = 2W[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]N_B(1 + \mu^2) = 2W[/latex]

Moment about contact point using rod geometry at [latex]\theta = 45^\circ[/latex]:
[latex]\mu = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\right) = \tan(22.5^\circ) \approx \mathbf{0.41}[/latex]

questions.question: A homogeneous, linearly elastic rod AB is connected to a linearly elastic spring BC in between the fixed supports at A and C, as shown in the figure. The cross-sectional area, modulus of elasticity, and coefficient of thermal expansion of rod AB are [latex]500 mm^2, 60 \times 10^3[/latex] MPa, and [latex]12 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex] ^\circ C[/latex], respectively. The stiffness [latex](k)[/latex] of spring BC is 2500 N/mm. The internal force (in kN) that will develop in the spring BC when the temperature of rod AB is increased by [latex]100 ^\circ C[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Given: Rod AB: Area [latex]A = 500[/latex] mm², [latex]E = 60 \times 10^3[/latex] MPa, [latex]\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ [/latex]C, Length [latex]L = 3[/latex] m = 3000 mm Spring BC: stiffness [latex]k = 2500[/latex] N/mm Temperature rise [latex]\Delta T = 100^\circ  C[/latex] Step 1  -  Free thermal expansion of rod AB: [latex]\delta_T = \alpha \cdot \Delta T \cdot L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 3000 = 3.6 \text{ mm}[/latex] Step 2  -  Compatibility: Let force in spring = P (compression in rod, tension in spring). Compression of rod: [latex]\delta_{rod} = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P \times 3000}{500 \times 60000} = \dfrac{P}{10000}[/latex] mm Extension of spring: [latex]\delta_{spring} = \dfrac{P}{k} = \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex] mm Step 3  -  Compatibility equation: [latex]\delta_T = \delta_{rod} + \delta_{spring}[/latex] [latex]3.6 = \dfrac{P}{10000} + \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex] [latex]3.6 = P\left(\dfrac{1}{10000} + \dfrac{4}{10000}\right) = \dfrac{5P}{10000}[/latex] [latex]P = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10000}{5} = 7200 \text{ N} = \mathbf{7.2 \text{ kN}}[/latex]
questions.topic: Properties of Metals, Stress and Strain
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Rod AB: Area [latex]A = 500[/latex] mm², [latex]E = 60 \times 10^3[/latex] MPa, [latex]\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}[/latex] per [latex]^\circ [/latex]C, Length [latex]L = 3[/latex] m = 3000 mm
Spring BC: stiffness [latex]k = 2500[/latex] N/mm
Temperature rise [latex]\Delta T = 100^\circ C[/latex]

Step 1 - Free thermal expansion of rod AB:
[latex]\delta_T = \alpha \cdot \Delta T \cdot L = 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 3000 = 3.6 \text{ mm}[/latex]

Step 2 - Compatibility:
Let force in spring = P (compression in rod, tension in spring).
Compression of rod: [latex]\delta_{rod} = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P \times 3000}{500 \times 60000} = \dfrac{P}{10000}[/latex] mm
Extension of spring: [latex]\delta_{spring} = \dfrac{P}{k} = \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex] mm

Step 3 - Compatibility equation:
[latex]\delta_T = \delta_{rod} + \delta_{spring}[/latex]
[latex]3.6 = \dfrac{P}{10000} + \dfrac{P}{2500}[/latex]
[latex]3.6 = P\left(\dfrac{1}{10000} + \dfrac{4}{10000}\right) = \dfrac{5P}{10000}[/latex]
[latex]P = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10000}{5} = 7200 \text{ N} = \mathbf{7.2 \text{ kN}}[/latex]

questions.question: The cross-section of a steel T-beam is shown in the figure where all dimensions are in mm. The plastic section modulus of the given cross-section is ______ [latex]\times 10^4 mm^3[/latex] (in integer).
questions.explanation: T-beam cross-section: Flange: 100 mm wide x 20 mm thick Web: 20 mm wide x 100 mm tall Total area: [latex]A_{flange} = 100 \times 20 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex] [latex]A_{web} = 20 \times 100 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex] [latex]A_{total} = 4000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex] Centroid from bottom: [latex]\bar{y} = \dfrac{2000 \times 110 + 2000 \times 50}{4000} = \dfrac{220000 + 100000}{4000} = \dfrac{320000}{4000} = 80 \text{ mm from bottom}[/latex] (Flange centroid = 100 + 20/2 = 110 mm; Web centroid = 100/2 = 50 mm from bottom) Plastic neutral axis (PNA): Divides total area equally [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] each half = 2000 mm² Area above PNA from top: Flange = 2000 mm² [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] PNA is exactly at flange-web junction (120 mm from top = top of web). Plastic section modulus [latex]Z_p[/latex]: [latex]Z_p = A_{top} \times \bar{y}_{top} + A_{bot} \times \bar{y}_{bot}[/latex] [latex]\bar{y}_{top}[/latex] (centroid of flange from PNA) = 10 mm [latex]\bar{y}_{bot}[/latex] (centroid of web from PNA) = 50 mm [latex]Z_p = 2000 \times 10 + 2000 \times 50 = 20000 + 100000 = 120000 \text{ mm}^3[/latex] [latex]= \mathbf{12 \times 10^4} \text{ mm}^3[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
T-beam cross-section:
Flange: 100 mm wide x 20 mm thick
Web: 20 mm wide x 100 mm tall

Total area:
[latex]A_{flange} = 100 \times 20 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]A_{web} = 20 \times 100 = 2000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]A_{total} = 4000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]

Centroid from bottom:
[latex]\bar{y} = \dfrac{2000 \times 110 + 2000 \times 50}{4000} = \dfrac{220000 + 100000}{4000} = \dfrac{320000}{4000} = 80 \text{ mm from bottom}[/latex]
(Flange centroid = 100 + 20/2 = 110 mm; Web centroid = 100/2 = 50 mm from bottom)

Plastic neutral axis (PNA): Divides total area equally [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] each half = 2000 mm²
Area above PNA from top: Flange = 2000 mm² [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] PNA is exactly at flange-web junction (120 mm from top = top of web).

Plastic section modulus [latex]Z_p[/latex]:
[latex]Z_p = A_{top} \times \bar{y}_{top} + A_{bot} \times \bar{y}_{bot}[/latex]
[latex]\bar{y}_{top}[/latex] (centroid of flange from PNA) = 10 mm
[latex]\bar{y}_{bot}[/latex] (centroid of web from PNA) = 50 mm
[latex]Z_p = 2000 \times 10 + 2000 \times 50 = 20000 + 100000 = 120000 \text{ mm}^3[/latex]
[latex]= \mathbf{12 \times 10^4} \text{ mm}^3[/latex]

questions.question: A fully-penetrating well of 20 cm diameter is provided in an unconfined aquifer. The height of the ground water table is 30 m from the bottom of the aquifer. After a long period of pumping at a rate of 63 [latex]m^3/s[/latex], the drawdown in the observation wells at 10 m and 100 m from the pumped well is 12 m and 11 m, respectively. The transmissibility (in [latex]m^2/s[/latex]) of the aquifer is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Given: Unconfined aquifer, pumping rate [latex]Q = 63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] (likely [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex], but using as given). [latex]H = 30 \ \text{m}[/latex] (initial water table) At [latex]r_1 = 10 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_1 = 12 \ \text{m}[/latex] [latex]h_1 = 30 - 12 = 18 \ \text{m}[/latex] At [latex]r_2 = 100 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_2 = 11 \ \text{m}[/latex] [latex]h_2 = 30 - 11 = 19 \ \text{m}[/latex] Dupuit's formula for an unconfined aquifer: [latex]Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}[/latex] Since transmissibility is [latex]T = K H[/latex], first determine [latex]K[/latex]: [latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (19^2 - 18^2)}{\ln(100/10)}[/latex] [latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (361 - 324)}{\ln(10)}[/latex] [latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K \times 37}{2.303}[/latex] [latex]K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.303}{\pi \times 37}[/latex] [latex]K = \dfrac{145.09}{116.24} = 1.248 \ \text{m/s}[/latex] Therefore,

[latex]T = K H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.44 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex] Note: The given discharge value of [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] is unrealistically high for this problem and is likely intended to be [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex]. Using the correct unit conversion, the transmissibility is approximately [latex]1.5  \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex] .
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Unconfined aquifer, pumping rate [latex]Q = 63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] (likely [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex], but using as given).
[latex]H = 30 \ \text{m}[/latex] (initial water table)
At [latex]r_1 = 10 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_1 = 12 \ \text{m}[/latex]
[latex]h_1 = 30 - 12 = 18 \ \text{m}[/latex]
At [latex]r_2 = 100 \ \text{m}[/latex], drawdown [latex]s_2 = 11 \ \text{m}[/latex]
[latex]h_2 = 30 - 11 = 19 \ \text{m}[/latex]

Dupuit's formula for an unconfined aquifer:
[latex]Q = \dfrac{\pi K (h_2^2 - h_1^2)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)}[/latex]

Since transmissibility is [latex]T = K H[/latex], first determine [latex]K[/latex]:
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (19^2 - 18^2)}{\ln(100/10)}[/latex]
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K (361 - 324)}{\ln(10)}[/latex]
[latex]63 = \dfrac{\pi K \times 37}{2.303}[/latex]
[latex]K = \dfrac{63 \times 2.303}{\pi \times 37}[/latex]
[latex]K = \dfrac{145.09}{116.24} = 1.248 \ \text{m/s}[/latex]

Therefore, [latex]T = K H = 1.248 \times 30 = 37.44 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex]

Note: The given discharge value of [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] is unrealistically high for this problem and is likely intended to be [latex]63 \ \text{m}^3/\text{hr}[/latex]. Using the correct unit conversion, the transmissibility is approximately [latex]1.5 \ \text{m}^2/\text{s}[/latex].

questions.question: A wide unlined channel carries sediment-free water. The depth of water is 1 m. The specific weight of water is 10 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. To prevent scouring, the maximum permissible tractive stress on bed is 10 [latex]kN/m^2[/latex]. The maximum slope of the channel bed to prevent scouring is 1 in [latex]n[/latex]. The value of [latex]n[/latex] is ______ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Given: Depth of water y = 1 m Specific weight of water [latex]\gamma_w = 10kN/m^3[/latex] Maximum permissible tractive stress [latex]\tau_c = 10N/m^2[/latex] Slope = 1 in n Tractive stress on bed: [latex]\tau_0 = \gamma_w \cdot y \cdot S[/latex] where S = bed slope = 1/n Setting [latex]\tau_0 = \tau_c[/latex]: [latex]10 \text{ N/m}^2 = 10000 \text{ N/m}^3 \times 1 \text{ m} \times \dfrac{1}{n}[/latex] [latex]10 = \dfrac{10000}{n}[/latex] [latex]n = \dfrac{10000}{10} = \mathbf{1000}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Depth of water y = 1 m
Specific weight of water [latex]\gamma_w = 10kN/m^3[/latex]
Maximum permissible tractive stress [latex]\tau_c = 10N/m^2[/latex]
Slope = 1 in n

Tractive stress on bed:
[latex]\tau_0 = \gamma_w \cdot y \cdot S[/latex]

where S = bed slope = 1/n

Setting [latex]\tau_0 = \tau_c[/latex]:
[latex]10 \text{ N/m}^2 = 10000 \text{ N/m}^3 \times 1 \text{ m} \times \dfrac{1}{n}[/latex]
[latex]10 = \dfrac{10000}{n}[/latex]
[latex]n = \dfrac{10000}{10} = \mathbf{1000}[/latex]

questions.question: A bridge with an expected life of 50 years is designed for a flood of 10000 [latex]m^3/s/[/latex] corresponding to the return period of 100 years. The risk associated with this design is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Risk formula: [latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n[/latex] Given: Design life [latex]n = 50[/latex] years Return period [latex]T = 100[/latex] years Calculation: [latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{100}\right)^{50} = 1 - (0.99)^{50}[/latex] [latex](0.99)^{50} = e^{50 \ln(0.99)} = e^{50 \times (-0.01005)} = e^{-0.5025} = 0.6050[/latex] [latex]R = 1 - 0.6050 = \mathbf{0.40}[/latex] There is approximately a 40% risk that the design flood will be exceeded at least once during the 50-year life of the bridge.
questions.explanation_html:
Risk formula:
[latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{T}\right)^n[/latex]

Given:
Design life [latex]n = 50[/latex] years
Return period [latex]T = 100[/latex] years

Calculation:
[latex]R = 1 - \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{100}\right)^{50} = 1 - (0.99)^{50}[/latex]

[latex](0.99)^{50} = e^{50 \ln(0.99)} = e^{50 \times (-0.01005)} = e^{-0.5025} = 0.6050[/latex]

[latex]R = 1 - 0.6050 = \mathbf{0.40}[/latex]

There is approximately a 40% risk that the design flood will be exceeded at least once during the 50-year life of the bridge.

questions.question: An infinite slope with slope angle [latex]\beta = 22 ^\circ[/latex] consists of soil with the following properties: Unit weight [latex]\gamma = 15.72 kN/m^3[/latex] Cohesion [latex]c' = 12[/latex] kPa Angle of internal friction [latex]\phi' = 15 ^\circ [/latex] The critical height of the slope (in m) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Use the factor of safety equation for an infinite slope

For a dry infinite slope,
[latex] F=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} [/latex]

At the critical height, the slope is on the verge of failure, hence [latex] F=1 [/latex]

Therefore, [latex] 1=\dfrac{c'}{\gamma H_c\sin\beta\cos\beta} +\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} [/latex]

Rearranging,
[latex] H_c= \dfrac{c'} {\gamma\sin\beta\cos\beta \left(1-\dfrac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta}\right)} [/latex]

Step 2: Substitute the given values

[latex] H_c= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times\sin22^\circ\times\cos22^\circ \left(1-\dfrac{\tan15^\circ}{\tan22^\circ}\right)} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{aligned} H_c &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3746\times0.9272 \left(1-\dfrac{0.2679}{0.4040}\right)}\\ &= \dfrac{12} {15.72\times0.3473\times0.3369}\\[4pt] &= \dfrac{12}{1.839}\\[4pt] &=6.52\ \text{m} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Hence, the critical height of the slope is [latex] H_c=6.52\ \text{m} [/latex]

questions.question: A circular pile of 600 mm diameter and 6 m length is embedded in a saturated clayey soil. Undrained cohesion of the soil is 80 kPa. Unit weight of the soil is 19.20 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The adhesion factor is 0.54. If the diameter of the pile is doubled to 1200 mm (keeping the length constant), the ratio of pile capacity of 1200 mm diameter pile to that of 600 mm diameter pile is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).

[latex]
L=6\ \text{m}
[/latex] Undrained cohesion:

[latex]
c_u=80\ \text{kPa}

where

[latex]

[/latex]

and

N_c=9

\qquad\text{and}\qquad
A_s=\pi DL

Q_u
=
9c_u\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right)
+
\alpha c_u(\pi DL)
[/latex] Since [latex]c_u[/latex] and [latex]\pi[/latex] are common,

[latex]

\frac{9}{4}D^2+\alpha LD

3.24+3.888

questions.explanation_html:
Given:

Pile length: [latex] L=6\ \text{m} [/latex]
Undrained cohesion: [latex] c_u=80\ \text{kPa} [/latex]
Unit weight of soil: [latex] \gamma=19.20\ \text{kN/m}^3 [/latex]
Adhesion factor: [latex] \alpha=0.54 [/latex]
Pile diameters: [latex] D_1=0.6\ \text{m}, \qquad D_2=1.2\ \text{m} [/latex]

Step 1: Ultimate capacity of a pile in clay

The ultimate pile capacity is given by [latex] Q_u=Q_b+Q_s [/latex] where [latex] Q_b=A_bN_cc_u [/latex] and [latex] Q_s=\alpha c_u A_s [/latex]

For clay, [latex] N_c=9 [/latex]

For a circular pile, [latex] A_b=\frac{\pi D^2}{4} \qquad\text{and}\qquad A_s=\pi DL [/latex]

Therefore,
[latex] Q_u = 9c_u\left(\frac{\pi D^2}{4}\right) + \alpha c_u(\pi DL) [/latex]

Since [latex]c_u[/latex] and [latex]\pi[/latex] are common, [latex] Q_u \propto \frac{9}{4}D^2+\alpha LD [/latex]

Step 2: Capacity of the 600 mm pile

[latex] Q_1 \propto \frac{9}{4}(0.6)^2+(0.54)(6)(0.6) [/latex]
[latex] Q_1 \propto 0.81+1.944 = 2.754 [/latex]

Step 3: Capacity of the 1200 mm pile

[latex] Q_2 \propto \frac{9}{4}(1.2)^2+(0.54)(6)(1.2) [/latex]
[latex] Q_2 \propto 3.24+3.888 = 7.128 [/latex]

Step 4: Compute the ratio

[latex] \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{7.128}{2.754} = 2.588 [/latex]

questions.question: A group of 25 circular piles is arranged in 5x5 uniform pattern in a soft clay soil with equal spacing in both directions. These are friction piles with negligible end bearing. Adhesion factor: [latex] \alpha=0.75 [/latex]
The piles are friction piles with negligible end bearing.

Step 1: Capacity of the pile group considering individual pile failure

Ultimate capacity of one pile is [latex] Q_{up}=\alpha c\pi dL [/latex]

Therefore, the ultimate capacity of 25 piles is [latex] Q_{ug1} = 25Q_{up} = 25\alpha c\pi dL [/latex]

The perimeter of the block is [latex] P=4B=4(4s+d) [/latex]

For block failure in clay, the ultimate capacity is obtained from the shear resistance developed along the perimeter of the block:
[latex] Q_{ug2} = cPL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L [/latex]

Step 3: Apply the condition of optimum spacing

[latex] Q_{ug1}=Q_{ug2} [/latex]
Therefore,
[latex] 25\alpha c\pi dL = c\,[4(4s+d)]\,L [/latex]

[latex] 25\alpha\pi d = 4(4s+d) [/latex]

questions.question: A shallow strip footing of width 2 m is embedded at a depth of 1.5 m below the ground surface in a homogeneous pure clay with an angle of internal friction zero. Consider unit weight of soil as 20 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex] and undrained cohesion of soil as  20 [latex]kN/m^2[/latex]. Due to rise of ground water table from far below the founding depth to the ground surface in monsoon season, the magnitude of percentage change in the net ultimate bearing capacity as per Terzaghi's theory is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Net ultimate bearing capacity for strip footing on pure clay ([latex]\phi = 0[/latex]) by Terzaghi: [latex]q_{net,ult} = c \cdot N_c + \gamma \cdot D_f(N_q - 1)[/latex] For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex]: [latex]N_c = 5.7[/latex], [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], [latex]N_\gamma = 0[/latex] [latex]q_{net,ult} = c \cdot N_c + \gamma \cdot D_f \cdot (1-1) = c \cdot N_c = 20 \times 5.7 = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex] After water table rises to ground surface: For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] pure clay: [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], so the [latex](N_q - 1)[/latex] term = 0 regardless of water table. The cohesion term [latex]c \cdot N_c[/latex] is unaffected by water table. [latex]q_{net,ult} = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex] (same as before) Percentage change = 0% Explanation: For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] soils, net ultimate bearing capacity is independent of unit weight, so water table rise has no effect.

For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex]: [latex]N_c = 5.7[/latex], [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], [latex]N_\gamma = 0[/latex]

[latex]q_{net,ult} = c \cdot N_c + \gamma \cdot D_f \cdot (1-1) = c \cdot N_c = 20 \times 5.7 = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex]

After water table rises to ground surface:
For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] pure clay: [latex]N_q = 1[/latex], so the [latex](N_q - 1)[/latex] term = 0 regardless of water table.
The cohesion term [latex]c \cdot N_c[/latex] is unaffected by water table.

[latex]q_{net,ult} = 114 \text{ kN/m}^2[/latex] (same as before)

Percentage change = 0%

Explanation: For [latex]\phi = 0[/latex] soils, net ultimate bearing capacity is independent of unit weight, so water table rise has no effect.

questions.question: In a bituminous mix, the percentage by weight of coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, filler, and bituminous binder is 58, 25, 12, and 5, respectively. The corresponding specific gravity of these materials is 2.68, 2.45, 2.42, and 1.15. The bulk specific gravity of the mix is 2.2. The Voids Filled with Bitumen (VFB, in percentage) is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Given: Mix proportions by weight: CA=58%, FA=25%, Filler=12%, Bitumen=5% Sp. gravity: [latex]G_{CA}=2.68[/latex], [latex]G_{FA}=2.45[/latex], [latex]G_{filler}=2.42[/latex], [latex]G_b=1.15[/latex] Bulk sp. gravity of mix [latex]G_m = 2.2[/latex] Step 1  -  Theoretical max sp. gravity [latex]G_{mm}[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{1}{G_{mm}} = \dfrac{0.58}{2.68} + \dfrac{0.25}{2.45} + \dfrac{0.12}{2.42} + \dfrac{0.05}{1.15} = 0.2164 + 0.1020 + 0.0496 + 0.0435 = 0.4115[/latex] [latex]G_{mm} = \dfrac{1}{0.4115} = 2.430[/latex] Step 2  -  Total air voids [latex]V_a[/latex]: [latex]V_a = \left(1 - \dfrac{G_m}{G_{mm}}\right) \times 100 = \left(1 - \dfrac{2.2}{2.430}\right) \times 100 = 9.47\%[/latex] Step 3  -  Volume of bitumen [latex]V_b[/latex]: [latex]V_b = \dfrac{G_m}{G_b} \times P_b = \dfrac{2.2}{1.15} \times 0.05 = 0.0957 = 9.57\%[/latex] Step 4  -  VMA (Voids in Mineral Aggregate): [latex]VMA = V_a + V_b = 9.47 + 9.57 = 19.04\%[/latex] Step 5  -  VFB: [latex]VFB = \dfrac{V_b}{VMA} \times 100 = \dfrac{9.57}{19.04} \times 100 = \mathbf{50\%}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: Mix proportions by weight: CA=58%, FA=25%, Filler=12%, Bitumen=5%
Sp. gravity: [latex]G_{CA}=2.68[/latex], [latex]G_{FA}=2.45[/latex], [latex]G_{filler}=2.42[/latex], [latex]G_b=1.15[/latex]
Bulk sp. gravity of mix [latex]G_m = 2.2[/latex]

Step 1 - Theoretical max sp. gravity [latex]G_{mm}[/latex]:
[latex]\dfrac{1}{G_{mm}} = \dfrac{0.58}{2.68} + \dfrac{0.25}{2.45} + \dfrac{0.12}{2.42} + \dfrac{0.05}{1.15} = 0.2164 + 0.1020 + 0.0496 + 0.0435 = 0.4115[/latex]
[latex]G_{mm} = \dfrac{1}{0.4115} = 2.430[/latex]

Step 2 - Total air voids [latex]V_a[/latex]:
[latex]V_a = \left(1 - \dfrac{G_m}{G_{mm}}\right) \times 100 = \left(1 - \dfrac{2.2}{2.430}\right) \times 100 = 9.47\%[/latex]

Step 3 - Volume of bitumen [latex]V_b[/latex]:
[latex]V_b = \dfrac{G_m}{G_b} \times P_b = \dfrac{2.2}{1.15} \times 0.05 = 0.0957 = 9.57\%[/latex]

Step 4 - VMA (Voids in Mineral Aggregate):
[latex]VMA = V_a + V_b = 9.47 + 9.57 = 19.04\%[/latex]

Step 5 - VFB:
[latex]VFB = \dfrac{V_b}{VMA} \times 100 = \dfrac{9.57}{19.04} \times 100 = \mathbf{50\%}[/latex]

questions.question: The intensity-duration relationship for rainfall on a rectangular plot ABCD of area 7 ha ([latex]1 \text{ ha} = 10^4 \text{ m}^2[/latex]) can be modelled by the following equation: [latex]I = \dfrac{25}{t + 10}[/latex] where [latex]I[/latex] is rainfall intensity (in cm/h) and [latex]t[/latex] is duration (in minutes)  of rainfall. The average runoff coefficient over the area is 0.60. The time of entry (in minutes) to the outfall from the corners A, B, C, and D is 10, 20, 15 and 25, respectively. The design flowrate (in [latex]m^3/h[/latex]) of the storm-sewer at the outfall is ______ (in integer).
questions.explanation: Given: Area [latex]= 7 ha = 70000 m^2[/latex], Runoff coefficient C = 0.60 Time of entry: A=10 min, B=20 min, C=15 min, D=25 min [latex]I = \dfrac{25}{t+10}[/latex] cm/h Rational method: [latex]Q = C \cdot I \cdot A[/latex] Design duration = longest time of concentration = 25 min (from corner D, since all corners must contribute for max flow) Intensity at t = 25 min: [latex]I = \dfrac{25}{25+10} = \dfrac{25}{35} = 0.7143 \text{ cm/h} = 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h}[/latex] Design flow: [latex]Q = C \times I \times A = 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h} \times 70000 \text{ m}^2[/latex] [latex]= 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \times 70000[/latex] [latex]= 0.60 \times 500 = \mathbf{300 \text{ m}^3/\text{h}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Area [latex]= 7 ha = 70000 m^2[/latex],
Runoff coefficient C = 0.60
Time of entry: A=10 min, B=20 min, C=15 min, D=25 min
[latex]I = \dfrac{25}{t+10}[/latex] cm/h

Rational method: [latex]Q = C \cdot I \cdot A[/latex]

[latex]I = \dfrac{25}{25+10} = \dfrac{25}{35} = 0.7143 \text{ cm/h} = 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h}[/latex]

Design flow:
[latex]Q = C \times I \times A = 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m/h} \times 70000 \text{ m}^2[/latex]
[latex]= 0.60 \times 7.143 \times 10^{-3} \times 70000[/latex]
[latex]= 0.60 \times 500 = \mathbf{300 \text{ m}^3/\text{h}}[/latex]

questions.question: A fifth-degree polynomial in [latex]x[/latex] is defined for [latex]x > 0[/latex]. All coefficients of the polynomial are positive. Identical step lengths are used for both methods. Following statements are made: (I) Forward difference method underestimates the true derivative. options.C: Statement (I) is TRUE and statement (II) is FALSE.

questions.explanation:
Given: A fifth-degree polynomial with all positive coefficients:

[latex]
f(x)=a_5x^5+a_4x^4+a_3x^3+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0
\qquad (a_i>0,\ x>0)
[/latex] We need to determine whether the first-order forward and backward difference approximations overestimate or underestimate the true derivative. Step 1: Examine the second derivative The first derivative is

[latex]
f'(x)
=
5a_5x^4+4a_4x^3+3a_3x^2+2a_2x+a_1
[/latex] The second derivative is

[latex]
f''(x)
=
20a_5x^3+12a_4x^2+6a_3x+2a_2
[/latex] Since all coefficients are positive and

[latex]
x>0,
[/latex]

we have

[latex]
f''(x)>0.
[/latex] Therefore, the function is convex (concave upward) . Step 2: Forward difference approximation The first-order forward difference formula is

[latex]
f'(x)
\approx
\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}.
[/latex] For a convex function,

[latex]
\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}
>
f'(x).
[/latex] Hence, the forward difference method overestimates the true derivative. Therefore, Statement (I) is FALSE . Step 3: Backward difference approximation The first-order backward difference formula is

[latex]
f'(x)
\approx
\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}.
[/latex] For a convex function,

[latex]
\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}
<
f'(x).
[/latex] Hence, the backward difference method underestimates the true derivative. Therefore, Statement (II) is FALSE .
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
A fifth-degree polynomial with all positive coefficients: [latex] f(x)=a_5x^5+a_4x^4+a_3x^3+a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0 \qquad (a_i>0,\ x>0) [/latex]

The first derivative is [latex] f'(x) = 5a_5x^4+4a_4x^3+3a_3x^2+2a_2x+a_1 [/latex]
The second derivative is [latex] f''(x) = 20a_5x^3+12a_4x^2+6a_3x+2a_2 [/latex]

Step 2: Forward difference approximation

The first-order forward difference formula is [latex] f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}. [/latex]
For a convex function, [latex] \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} > f'(x). [/latex]
Hence, the forward difference method overestimates the true derivative.

Therefore, Statement (I) is FALSE.

Step 3: Backward difference approximation

For a convex function, [latex] \frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h} < f'(x). [/latex]
Hence, the backward difference method underestimates the true derivative.

Therefore, Statement (II) is FALSE.

questions.question: Periodic function [latex]f(x)[/latex] is given below: [latex]f(x) = \begin{cases} -1, & \text{when } -\pi < x < 0 \\ 1, & \text{when } 0 < x < \pi \end{cases}[/latex];  [latex]f(x + 2\pi) = f(x)[/latex] The CORRECT option representing the Fourier series expansion of [latex]f(x)[/latex] is:

Fourier sine coefficients: [latex]b_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} 1 \cdot \sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[-\dfrac{\cos(nx)}{n}\right]_0^{\pi} = \dfrac{2}{n\pi}(1 - \cos n\pi)[/latex] For odd n: [latex]\cos(n\pi) = -1[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]b_n = \dfrac{4}{n\pi}[/latex] For even n: [latex]\cos(n\pi) = 1[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]b_n = 0[/latex] Therefore: [latex]f(x) = \dfrac{4}{\pi}\left[\sin x + \dfrac{\sin 3x}{3} + \dfrac{\sin 5x}{5} + \cdots\right][/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
The function is an odd function (antisymmetric about [latex]x = 0[/latex]), so its Fourier series contains only sine terms (no cosine terms, no constant).

Fourier sine coefficients:
[latex]b_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi} 1 \cdot \sin(nx)\,dx = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[-\dfrac{\cos(nx)}{n}\right]_0^{\pi} = \dfrac{2}{n\pi}(1 - \cos n\pi)[/latex]

Role of algae in wastewater treatment: In an oxidation pond (waste stabilization pond), a natural symbiotic relationship exists between algae and bacteria. Bacteria decompose organic matter (BOD) in wastewater using dissolved oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water, ammonia, and other by-products. Algae utilize sunlight, carbon dioxide, and nutrients released during bacterial decomposition to carry out photosynthesis and generate oxygen. The photosynthetic reaction can be represented as:

Thus, the algae-bacteria symbiosis forms the fundamental mechanism of treatment in oxidation ponds. Cyclone separator: A purely physical device that removes particulate matter using centrifugal force; no biological activity is involved. Septic tank: Treatment occurs under anaerobic conditions. Since sunlight and oxygen are absent, algae cannot grow and therefore play no role in the process. Hence, algae are mainly associated with the operation of an oxidation pond.

questions.question: Let [latex]f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x^3 & \sin x & \cos x \\ 6 & -1 & 0 \\ p & p^2 & p^3 \end{vmatrix}[/latex] where [latex]p[/latex] is a constant. The value of [latex]\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3} f(x)[/latex] at [latex]x = 0[/latex] is:
questions.explanation: Key observation: Expanding the determinant along Row 2 (constants), we get: [latex]f(x) = 6 \cdot M_{21} + (-1) \cdot M_{22} + 0 \cdot M_{23}[/latex] where [latex]M_{ij}[/latex] are cofactors. The third derivative [latex]\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}f(x)[/latex] only acts on terms involving [latex]x[/latex]. Expanding along Row 1: [latex]f(x) = x^3(-p^3 - 0) - \sin x(6p^3 - 0) + \cos x(6p^2 - (-p))[/latex] [latex]= -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + \cos x(6p^2 + p)[/latex] Taking third derivative: [latex]f(x) = -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + (6p^2 + p)\cos x[/latex] [latex]f'(x) = -3p^3 x^2 - 6p^3 \cos x - (6p^2+p)\sin x[/latex] [latex]f''(x) = -6p^3 x + 6p^3 \sin x - (6p^2+p)\cos x[/latex] [latex]f'''(x) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 \cos x + (6p^2+p)\sin x[/latex] At [latex]x=0[/latex]:  [latex]f'''(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3(1) + (6p^2+p)(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 = \mathbf{0}[/latex] The result is 0, which is independent of p .
questions.explanation_html:
Key observation: Expanding the determinant along Row 2 (constants), we get:
[latex]f(x) = 6 \cdot M_{21} + (-1) \cdot M_{22} + 0 \cdot M_{23}[/latex]
where [latex]M_{ij}[/latex] are cofactors.

The third derivative [latex]\dfrac{d^3}{dx^3}f(x)[/latex] only acts on terms involving [latex]x[/latex].

Expanding along Row 1:
[latex]f(x) = x^3(-p^3 - 0) - \sin x(6p^3 - 0) + \cos x(6p^2 - (-p))[/latex]
[latex]= -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + \cos x(6p^2 + p)[/latex]

Taking third derivative:
[latex]f(x) = -p^3 x^3 - 6p^3 \sin x + (6p^2 + p)\cos x[/latex]
[latex]f'(x) = -3p^3 x^2 - 6p^3 \cos x - (6p^2+p)\sin x[/latex]
[latex]f''(x) = -6p^3 x + 6p^3 \sin x - (6p^2+p)\cos x[/latex]
[latex]f'''(x) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 \cos x + (6p^2+p)\sin x[/latex]

At [latex]x=0[/latex]: [latex]f'''(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3(1) + (6p^2+p)(0) = -6p^3 + 6p^3 = \mathbf{0}[/latex]

The result is 0, which is independent of p.

questions.question: Vector field [latex]\vec{V}[/latex] is defined as: [latex]\vec{V} = 3x^2yz\,\hat{i} - 5xy\,\hat{j} + 6yz^2\,\hat{k}[/latex] The curl of [latex]\vec{V}[/latex] at point [latex](2, -1, 1)[/latex] is:
questions.explanation: Given: [latex]\vec{V} = 3x^2yz\,\hat{i} - 5xy\,\hat{j} + 6yz^2\,\hat{k}[/latex] Curl formula: [latex]\nabla \times \vec{V} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial/\partial x & \partial/\partial y & \partial/\partial z \\ V_x & V_y & V_z \end{vmatrix}[/latex] Components: [latex]V_x = 3x^2yz,\ V_y = -5xy,\ V_z = 6yz^2[/latex] [latex]\hat{i}[/latex] component: [latex]\dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial z} = \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial z} = 6z^2 - 0 = 6z^2[/latex] At (2,−1,1): [latex]6(1)^2 = 6[/latex] [latex]\hat{j}[/latex] component: [latex]\dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial x} = 3x^2y - 0 = 3x^2y[/latex] At (2,−1,1): [latex]3(4)(-1) = -12[/latex] [latex]\hat{k}[/latex] component: [latex]\dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial y} = -5y - 3x^2z[/latex] At (2,−1,1): [latex]-5(-1) - 3(4)(1) = 5 - 12 = -7[/latex] Curl = [latex]6\hat{i} - 12\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]\vec{V} = 3x^2yz\,\hat{i} - 5xy\,\hat{j} + 6yz^2\,\hat{k}[/latex]

Curl formula:
[latex]\nabla \times \vec{V} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ \partial/\partial x & \partial/\partial y & \partial/\partial z \\ V_x & V_y & V_z \end{vmatrix}[/latex]

Components: [latex]V_x = 3x^2yz,\ V_y = -5xy,\ V_z = 6yz^2[/latex]

[latex]\hat{i}[/latex] component:
[latex]\dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial z} = \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial z} = 6z^2 - 0 = 6z^2[/latex]
At (2,−1,1): [latex]6(1)^2 = 6[/latex]

[latex]\hat{j}[/latex] component:
[latex]\dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial V_z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial z} - \dfrac{\partial(6yz^2)}{\partial x} = 3x^2y - 0 = 3x^2y[/latex]
At (2,−1,1): [latex]3(4)(-1) = -12[/latex]

[latex]\hat{k}[/latex] component:
[latex]\dfrac{\partial V_y}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial V_x}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial(-5xy)}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial(3x^2yz)}{\partial y} = -5y - 3x^2z[/latex]
At (2,−1,1): [latex]-5(-1) - 3(4)(1) = 5 - 12 = -7[/latex]

Curl = [latex]6\hat{i} - 12\hat{j} - 7\hat{k}[/latex]
