questions.question: Consider the following statements with respect to rigid pavements: Statement-1: Bottom-up cracking (BUC) in rigid pavements is caused at the edge of the slab due to combined effect of single or tandem rear axle load and positive temperature differential. Statement-2: Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC) in rigid pavements is caused due to repeated cycles of axle loads and negative temperature differential. The CORRECT option is:

options.B: Statement-1 is TRUE but Statement-2 is FALSE.
options.C: Statement-1 is FALSE but Statement-2 is TRUE.

questions.explanation: Statement 1  -  Bottom-up cracking (BUC): BUC initiates at the bottom of the slab where tensile stresses are maximum. It is caused by: Heavy axle loads (single or tandem rear axle) causing bending stress  -  maximum tension at bottom Positive temperature differential (top > bottom) causes the slab to curl upward at edges/corners, making the slab unsupported at edges  -  this increases bottom tensile stress Statement 1 is TRUE . Statement 2  -  Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC): TDC initiates at the top surface of the slab and propagates downward. It is caused by: Repeated cycles of axle loads on the slab surface Negative temperature differential (bottom > top) causes slab to curl downward at edges  -  top surface is in tension, initiating top-down cracks Statement 2 is TRUE . Therefore, Both statements are TRUE.
questions.explanation_html:
Statement 1 - Bottom-up cracking (BUC):
BUC initiates at the bottom of the slab where tensile stresses are maximum. It is caused by:
Heavy axle loads (single or tandem rear axle) causing bending stress - maximum tension at bottom
Positive temperature differential (top > bottom) causes the slab to curl upward at edges/corners, making the slab unsupported at edges - this increases bottom tensile stress
Statement 1 is TRUE.

Statement 2 - Top-down fatigue cracking (TDC):
TDC initiates at the top surface of the slab and propagates downward. It is caused by:
Repeated cycles of axle loads on the slab surface
Negative temperature differential (bottom > top) causes slab to curl downward at edges - top surface is in tension, initiating top-down cracks
Statement 2 is TRUE.

Therefore, Both statements are TRUE.

questions.question: A shallow footing is subjected to a vertical load. Within the elastic limit of the underlying soil, the TRUE statement(s) is/are:

options.A: Vertical displacement below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.B: Vertical contact pressure below a rigid shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.C: Vertical displacement below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.
options.D: Vertical contact pressure below a flexible shallow footing is uniform in clay as well as sand.

questions.explanation: Behavior of rigid vs flexible footings: (A) TRUE  -  Rigid footing, uniform settlement: A rigid footing does not deform, so all points beneath it settle by the same amount (uniform vertical displacement), regardless of soil type (clay or sand). (B) FALSE  -  Rigid footing, contact pressure: Contact pressure under a rigid footing is NOT uniform : In clay: parabolic (higher at edges) In sand: higher at centre, lower at edges The contact pressure distribution varies with soil type. (C) FALSE  -  Flexible footing, uniform settlement: A flexible footing conforms to the soil surface, so settlement is non-uniform -  higher at centre, lower at edges (in most soils). (D) TRUE  -  Flexible footing, uniform contact pressure: A perfectly flexible footing applies a uniform contact pressure equal to the applied load per unit area (like a uniformly loaded mattress).
questions.explanation_html:
Behavior of rigid vs flexible footings:

(A) TRUE - Rigid footing, uniform settlement:
A rigid footing does not deform, so all points beneath it settle by the same amount (uniform vertical displacement), regardless of soil type (clay or sand).

(B) FALSE - Rigid footing, contact pressure:
Contact pressure under a rigid footing is NOT uniform:
In clay: parabolic (higher at edges)
In sand: higher at centre, lower at edges
The contact pressure distribution varies with soil type.

(C) FALSE - Flexible footing, uniform settlement:
A flexible footing conforms to the soil surface, so settlement is non-uniform - higher at centre, lower at edges (in most soils).

(D) TRUE - Flexible footing, uniform contact pressure:
A perfectly flexible footing applies a uniform contact pressure equal to the applied load per unit area (like a uniformly loaded mattress).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are TRUE with respect to the type of stresses to be considered for the design of rigid pavements?

options.A: Warping stress due to temperature differential between top and bottom of the pavement slab as a result of daily variation in temperature
options.B: Frictional stress due to overall increase or decrease in temperature of the pavement slab as a result of seasonal variation in temperature
options.C: Critical stress obtained as the maximum of the wheel load stress, the warping stress, and the frictional stress
options.D: Critical stress obtained as the sum of wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner of the pavement slab

questions.explanation_html:
Option A:
Warping stresses develop in a rigid pavement due to the temperature difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the slab during a day.
The temperature gradient causes the slab to curl upward or downward, producing warping stresses.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option A is TRUE}} [/latex]
Option B:
Seasonal changes in temperature cause the entire slab to expand or contract. Since the slab movement is restrained by subgrade friction, frictional stresses are developed.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option B is TRUE}} [/latex]
Option C:

In rigid pavement design, the critical tensile stress is not obtained by taking the maximum of wheel load stress, warping stress, and frictional stress individually.
The design stress is generally obtained by combining the wheel load stress and temperature-related stresses at the critical location.
Hence, taking only the maximum of the individual stresses is incorrect.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option C is FALSE}} [/latex]
Option D:

Wheel load stresses at edge, interior, and corner do not occur simultaneously at the same location.
The critical condition is obtained by considering the most critical loading position, not by summing all three stresses.

Therefore, [latex] \boxed{\text{Option D is FALSE}} [/latex]

questions.question: Consider differential equation [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex] with the condition [latex]y = 0[/latex] at [latex]x = 0[/latex]. The value of [latex]y[/latex] at [latex]x = 1.0[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given ODE: [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex], [latex]y(0) = 0[/latex] Step 1  -  This is a linear first-order ODE. Rewrite: [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex] Step 2  -  Integrating factor (IF): [latex]IF = e^{\int x\,dx} = e^{x^2/2}[/latex] Step 3  -  Multiply both sides by IF: [latex]\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y \cdot e^{x^2/2}\right) = x \cdot e^{x^2/2}[/latex] Step 4  -  Integrate both sides: [latex]y \cdot e^{x^2/2} = \int x \cdot e^{x^2/2}\,dx[/latex] Let [latex]t = x^2/2[/latex], [latex]dt = x\,dx[/latex]: [latex]= \int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{x^2/2} + C[/latex] Step 5  -  General solution: [latex]y = 1 + Ce^{-x^2/2}[/latex] Step 6  -  Apply initial condition y(0) = 0: [latex]0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1[/latex] [latex]y = 1 - e^{-x^2/2}[/latex] Step 7  -  Find y at x = 1: [latex]y(1) = 1 - e^{-1/2} = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.6065 = \mathbf{0.39}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given ODE: [latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex], [latex]y(0) = 0[/latex]

Step 1 - This is a linear first-order ODE. Rewrite:
[latex]\dfrac{dy}{dx} + xy = x[/latex]

Step 2 - Integrating factor (IF):
[latex]IF = e^{\int x\,dx} = e^{x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 3 - Multiply both sides by IF:
[latex]\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(y \cdot e^{x^2/2}\right) = x \cdot e^{x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 4 - Integrate both sides:
[latex]y \cdot e^{x^2/2} = \int x \cdot e^{x^2/2}\,dx[/latex]
Let [latex]t = x^2/2[/latex], [latex]dt = x\,dx[/latex]:
[latex]= \int e^t\,dt = e^t + C = e^{x^2/2} + C[/latex]

Step 5 - General solution:
[latex]y = 1 + Ce^{-x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 6 - Apply initial condition y(0) = 0:
[latex]0 = 1 + C \Rightarrow C = -1[/latex]
[latex]y = 1 - e^{-x^2/2}[/latex]

Step 7 - Find y at x = 1:
[latex]y(1) = 1 - e^{-1/2} = 1 - e^{-0.5} = 1 - 0.6065 = \mathbf{0.39}[/latex]

questions.question: The age (in years) of a population is normally distributed with a mean of 36 and standard deviation of 12. The height (in cm) of the same population is also normally distributed with a mean of 160 and standard deviation of 10. If the probability of age greater than 50 years is equal to the probability of height greater than [latex]h[/latex], the value of [latex]h[/latex] (in cm) is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Age distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_a = 36[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_a = 12[/latex] Height distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_h = 160[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_h = 10[/latex] Step 1  -  Find z-score for age > 50: [latex]z = \dfrac{50 - 36}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = 1.1\overline{6} \approx 1.167[/latex] Step 2  -  The probability P(age > 50) = P(Z > 1.167) This equals the same probability for height: [latex]P(\text{height} > h) = P(Z > 1.167)[/latex] Step 3  -  Find h using the same z-score: [latex]\dfrac{h - 160}{10} = 1.167[/latex] [latex]h = 160 + 1.167 \times 10 = 160 + 11.67 = \mathbf{171.67 \text{ cm}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Age distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_a = 36[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_a = 12[/latex]
Height distribution: Mean [latex]\mu_h = 160[/latex], SD [latex]\sigma_h = 10[/latex]

Step 1 - Find z-score for age > 50:
[latex]z = \dfrac{50 - 36}{12} = \dfrac{14}{12} = 1.1\overline{6} \approx 1.167[/latex]

Step 2 - The probability P(age > 50) = P(Z > 1.167)
This equals the same probability for height:
[latex]P(\text{height} > h) = P(Z > 1.167)[/latex]

Step 3 - Find h using the same z-score:
[latex]\dfrac{h - 160}{10} = 1.167[/latex]
[latex]h = 160 + 1.167 \times 10 = 160 + 11.67 = \mathbf{171.67 \text{ cm}}[/latex]

questions.question: A 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep rectangular concrete beam is prestressed by means of 4 high-tensile tendons, each of 14 mm diameter. The centre of the tendons is 200 mm from the soffit of the beam. The effective stress in each tendon is 700 N/mm². The maximum bending moment (in kN·m), that can be applied to the section without causing tension at the soffit of the beam due to prestressing only, is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place). Use [latex]\pi = 3.14[/latex]
questions.explanation: Given: Beam: 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep. 4 tendons of 14 mm diameter, centred 200 mm from soffit. Effective stress  [latex]= 700 N/mm^2. \; \pi = 3.14[/latex] Step 1  -  Area of each tendon: [latex]A_t = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 14^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 196}{4} = \dfrac{615.44}{4} = 153.86 \text{ mm}^2[/latex] Step 2  -  Total prestress force P: [latex]P = 4 \times A_t \times f_{pe} = 4 \times 153.86 \times 700 = 430808 \text{ N} \approx 430.8 \text{ kN}[/latex] Step 3  -  Eccentricity e (from centroid to tendon): Centroid of beam from soffit = 600/2 = 300 mm [latex]e = 300 - 200 = 100 \text{ mm}[/latex] Step 4  -  Section modulus (bottom fibre): [latex]Z_b = \dfrac{bD^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 600^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 360000}{6} = 15 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3[/latex] Step 5  -  Maximum BM without tension at soffit: Stress at soffit = [latex]\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b} - \dfrac{M}{Z_b} \geq 0[/latex] [latex]M \leq \left(\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b}\right) \times Z_b = P \cdot \dfrac{Z_b}{A} + P \cdot e[/latex] [latex]A = 250 \times 600 = 150000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex] [latex]M \leq 430.8 \times \dfrac{15 \times 10^6}{150000} + 430.8 \times 100[/latex] [latex]M \leq 430.8 \times 100 + 430.8 \times 100 = 43080 + 43080 = 86160 \text{ kN mm} = 86.2 \text{ kN m}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: Beam: 250 mm wide x 600 mm deep. 4 tendons of 14 mm diameter, centred 200 mm from soffit. Effective stress [latex]= 700 N/mm^2. \; \pi = 3.14[/latex]

Step 1 - Area of each tendon:
[latex]A_t = \dfrac{\pi d^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 14^2}{4} = \dfrac{3.14 \times 196}{4} = \dfrac{615.44}{4} = 153.86 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]

Step 2 - Total prestress force P:
[latex]P = 4 \times A_t \times f_{pe} = 4 \times 153.86 \times 700 = 430808 \text{ N} \approx 430.8 \text{ kN}[/latex]

Step 3 - Eccentricity e (from centroid to tendon):
Centroid of beam from soffit = 600/2 = 300 mm
[latex]e = 300 - 200 = 100 \text{ mm}[/latex]

Step 4 - Section modulus (bottom fibre):
[latex]Z_b = \dfrac{bD^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 600^2}{6} = \dfrac{250 \times 360000}{6} = 15 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3[/latex]

Step 5 - Maximum BM without tension at soffit:
Stress at soffit = [latex]\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b} - \dfrac{M}{Z_b} \geq 0[/latex]
[latex]M \leq \left(\dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{Pe}{Z_b}\right) \times Z_b = P \cdot \dfrac{Z_b}{A} + P \cdot e[/latex]
[latex]A = 250 \times 600 = 150000 \text{ mm}^2[/latex]
[latex]M \leq 430.8 \times \dfrac{15 \times 10^6}{150000} + 430.8 \times 100[/latex]
[latex]M \leq 430.8 \times 100 + 430.8 \times 100 = 43080 + 43080 = 86160 \text{ kN mm} = 86.2 \text{ kN m}[/latex]

questions.question:
A rigid-jointed portal frame, shown in the figure, consists of beam and columns of 
equal length [latex]L[/latex]. The frame has a fixed support at one end and a roller support at the other end. The frame is subjected to a uniformly distributed load [latex]w[/latex] and a lateral load [latex]P[/latex] as shown in the figure. The plastic moment capacity of the beam and column sections is [latex]M_p[/latex]. Consider a combined beam-column mechanism for plastic collapse. By applying the virtual work equation corresponding to the combined plastic collapse mechanism, [latex]M_p[/latex] is expressed as [latex]M_p = C_1 PL + C_2 wL^2[/latex] where [latex]C_1[/latex] and [latex]C_2[/latex] are constants. The value of [latex](C_1/C_2)[/latex] is ______ (in integer).

L,

[latex]

[latex]
=P(L\theta).

The vertical displacement at the beam center is

[latex]

For a uniformly distributed load,

=

[latex]
\dfrac{\delta}{2}.
[/latex] Therefore,

[latex]
W_w
=
wL\left(\dfrac{L\theta}{4}\right)
=
\dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4}.

[latex]
\theta

[latex]
\theta

[latex]
\theta

[latex]
2\theta

[latex]
W_i
=
M_p(\theta+\theta+\theta+2\theta)
[/latex]

[latex]
=
5M_p\theta.
[/latex] Step 5: Apply virtual work equation [latex]
W_P+W_w=W_i
[/latex] [latex]
PL\theta+\dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4}
=
5M_p\theta.
[/latex] Cancelling

[latex]
\theta,
[/latex] [latex]
5M_p
=
PL+\dfrac{wL^2}{4}.
[/latex] Therefore,

[latex]
M_p
=
\dfrac{1}{5}PL+\frac{1}{20}wL^2.
[/latex] Comparing with

[latex]
M_p=C_1PL+C_2wL^2,
[/latex] we get

[latex]
C_1=\dfrac{1}{5},
\qquad
C_2=\dfrac{1}{20}.
[/latex] Hence,

[latex]
\dfrac{C_1}{C_2}
=
\dfrac{1/5}{1/20}
=
4.
[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Step 1: Identify the collapse mechanism
For the combined beam-column mechanism, plastic hinges form at:
- Left column base (fixed support)
- Left beam-column joint
- Right beam-column joint
- One plastic hinge at the mid-span of the beam
Thus, total plastic hinges formed: [latex] 4 [/latex]
Since the frame has degree of indeterminacy 3, four plastic hinges are required to form a mechanism.

Step 2: External work done by lateral load
Let the sway displacement at the beam level be [latex] \Delta. [/latex] Let the rotation of the columns be [latex] \theta. [/latex] Since column height is [latex] L, [/latex] [latex] \Delta=L\theta. [/latex] External work done by the lateral load: [latex] W_P=P\Delta [/latex] [latex] =P(L\theta). [/latex]
Step 3: External work done by UDL

Due to the beam mechanism, a plastic hinge forms at mid-span. The vertical displacement at the beam center is [latex] \delta=\dfrac{L}{2}\theta. [/latex] For a uniformly distributed load, [latex] W_w = wL\left(\dfrac{\delta}{2}\right) [/latex]
since the average displacement of the load is [latex] \dfrac{\delta}{2}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] W_w = wL\left(\dfrac{L\theta}{4}\right) = \dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4}. [/latex]
Step 4: Internal work
Plastic hinge rotations are:
Left base hinge: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Left beam-column joint: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Right beam-column joint: [latex] \theta [/latex]
Mid-span beam hinge: [latex] 2\theta [/latex]
Hence, [latex] W_i = M_p(\theta+\theta+\theta+2\theta) [/latex] [latex] = 5M_p\theta. [/latex]
Step 5: Apply virtual work equation
[latex] W_P+W_w=W_i [/latex]
[latex] PL\theta+\dfrac{wL^2\theta}{4} = 5M_p\theta. [/latex]
Cancelling [latex] \theta, [/latex]
[latex] 5M_p = PL+\dfrac{wL^2}{4}. [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] M_p = \dfrac{1}{5}PL+\frac{1}{20}wL^2. [/latex]
Comparing with [latex] M_p=C_1PL+C_2wL^2, [/latex]
we get [latex] C_1=\dfrac{1}{5}, \qquad C_2=\dfrac{1}{20}. [/latex]
Hence, [latex] \dfrac{C_1}{C_2} = \dfrac{1/5}{1/20} = 4. [/latex]

questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Axial rigidity of both bars: [latex] AE=20000\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Applied load: [latex] P=20\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Gap between D and F: [latex] g=2\ \text{mm}=0.002\ \text{m} [/latex]
Lengths: [latex] BD=10\ \text{m} \qquad FG=5\ \text{m} [/latex]
Step 1: Check whether the gap closes

If only the left bar acts, the displacement of point D due to the 20 kN load is
[latex] \delta_D = \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{20\times10}{20000} = 0.01\ \text{m} = 10\ \text{mm} [/latex]
Since [latex] 10\ \text{mm}>2\ \text{mm}, [/latex] the gap closes and the right bar also starts carrying load.

Step 2: Let the final reactions be
[latex] R_B = \text{reaction at B} [/latex]
[latex] R_G = \text{reaction at G} [/latex]
From equilibrium, [latex] R_B+R_G=20 \;\; ...(1) [/latex]
Step 3: Apply compatibility condition
After contact, the displacement of D must be equal to:
Gap closed [latex] (2\ \text{mm}) [/latex] plus
Compression of the right bar FG.
Compression of left bar: [latex] \delta_L = \dfrac{R_B(10)}{20000} [/latex]
Compression of right bar: [latex] \delta_R = \dfrac{R_G(5)}{20000} [/latex]
Hence, [latex] \delta_L = 0.002+\delta_R [/latex]
Substituting, [latex] \dfrac{10R_B}{20000} = 0.002+\dfrac{5R_G}{20000} [/latex]
Multiplying by 20000, [latex] 10R_B = 40+5R_G \; \; ...(2) [/latex]
Using Equation (1), [latex] R_G=20-R_B [/latex]
Substituting into Equation (2),
[latex] 10R_B = 40+5(20-R_B) [/latex]
[latex] 10R_B = 140-5R_B [/latex]
[latex] 15R_B=140 [/latex]
[latex] R_B=15.33\ \text{kN} [/latex]
Therefore, [latex] R_B\approx16\ \text{kN} [/latex] to the nearest integer.

questions.question:
A simply-supported rectangular reinforced concrete beam has a width 250 mm and 
an overall depth 600 mm. The effective span of the beam is 6.23 m. The beam 
carries a live load of 5 kN/m and super imposed dead load of 5 kN/m, in addition to 
its own weight. The unit weight of reinforced concrete is 25 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. Consider the 
load factor of 1.5 for all stated loads. The design bending moment (in kN·m) for the limit state of collapse is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: b = 250 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm, span L = 6.23 m Live load = 5 kN/m, SIDL = 5 kN/m, Unit weight of RC = 25 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex], Load factor = 1.5 Step 1  -  Self weight of beam: [latex]w_{SW} = b \times D \times \gamma = 0.25 \times 0.60 \times 25 = 3.75 \text{ kN/m}[/latex] Step 2  -  Total factored load: [latex]w_u = 1.5 \times (w_{LL} + w_{SIDL} + w_{SW}) = 1.5 \times (5 + 5 + 3.75) = 1.5 \times 13.75 = 20.625 \text{ kN/m}[/latex] Step 3  -  Design bending moment (simply supported): [latex]M_u = \dfrac{w_u L^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times (6.23)^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times 38.81}{8} = \dfrac{800.5}{8} = \mathbf{100.06 \text{ kN.m}}[/latex]

Step 2 - Total factored load:
[latex]w_u = 1.5 \times (w_{LL} + w_{SIDL} + w_{SW}) = 1.5 \times (5 + 5 + 3.75) = 1.5 \times 13.75 = 20.625 \text{ kN/m}[/latex]

Step 3 - Design bending moment (simply supported):
[latex]M_u = \dfrac{w_u L^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times (6.23)^2}{8} = \dfrac{20.625 \times 38.81}{8} = \dfrac{800.5}{8} = \mathbf{100.06 \text{ kN.m}}[/latex]

questions.question: Width (in m) of a rectangular channel required to carry a discharge of [latex]96 m^3/s[/latex] at a critical depth of 9.8 m is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places). Use  acceleration due to gravity [latex]g = 9.8 m/s^2[/latex]
questions.explanation: At critical depth in a rectangular channel: [latex]Q = A\sqrt{g \cdot y_c}[/latex] where [latex]A = B \times y_c[/latex] for rectangular channel Given:  [latex]Q = 96 m^3/s, y_c = 9.8 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2[/latex] Formula: [latex]Q = B \cdot y_c \cdot \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}[/latex] Solving for B: [latex]B = \dfrac{Q}{y_c \sqrt{g \cdot y_c}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times \sqrt{9.8 \times 9.8}} = \dfrac{96}{9.8 \times 9.8} = \dfrac{96}{96.04} \approx \mathbf{1.00 \text{ m}}[/latex]

[latex]Q = A\sqrt{g \cdot y_c}[/latex] where [latex]A = B \times y_c[/latex] for rectangular channel

Given: [latex]Q = 96 m^3/s, y_c = 9.8 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2[/latex]

questions.question: The cross section of a 0.5 m wide vertical gate holding water and oil is shown in the figure. The unit weights of water and oil are [latex]10 kN/m^3[/latex] and [latex]7.5 kN/m^3[/latex], respectively. The horizontal hydrostatic force (in kN) acting on the vertical gate is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: Gate width = 0.5 m; Oil depth = 0.5 m (top); Water depth = 1.0 m (bottom) [latex]γ_{oil} = 7.5 kN/m^3, γ_{water} = 10 kN/m^3[/latex] Horizontal hydrostatic force = pressure at centroid x area Force due to oil layer (0 to 0.5 m depth): Centroid of oil at depth 0.25 m from oil surface. Pressure at centroid = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.25 = 7.5 \times 0.25 = 1.875 kN/m^2[/latex] Area = [latex]0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 m^2[/latex] [latex]F_{oil} = 1.875 \times 0.25 = 0.469[/latex] kN Force due to water layer (0.5 m to 1.5 m depth from oil surface): Pressure at top of water = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75 kN/m^2[/latex] Pressure at bottom = [latex]3.75 + \gamma_w \times 1.0 = 3.75 + 10 = 13.75 kN/m^2[/latex] Average pressure = [latex](3.75 + 13.75)/2 = 8.75 kN/m^2[/latex] Area = [latex]1.0 \times 0.5 = 0.5 m^2[/latex] [latex]F_{water} = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375[/latex] kN Total force: [latex]F = F_{oil} + F_{water} = 0.469 + 4.375 = \mathbf{4.84 \text{ kN}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: Gate width = 0.5 m; Oil depth = 0.5 m (top); Water depth = 1.0 m (bottom)
[latex]γ_{oil} = 7.5 kN/m^3, γ_{water} = 10 kN/m^3[/latex]

Horizontal hydrostatic force = pressure at centroid x area

Force due to oil layer (0 to 0.5 m depth):
Centroid of oil at depth 0.25 m from oil surface.
Pressure at centroid = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.25 = 7.5 \times 0.25 = 1.875 kN/m^2[/latex]
Area = [latex]0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25 m^2[/latex]
[latex]F_{oil} = 1.875 \times 0.25 = 0.469[/latex] kN

Force due to water layer (0.5 m to 1.5 m depth from oil surface):
Pressure at top of water = [latex]\gamma_{oil} \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 0.5 = 3.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Pressure at bottom = [latex]3.75 + \gamma_w \times 1.0 = 3.75 + 10 = 13.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Average pressure = [latex](3.75 + 13.75)/2 = 8.75 kN/m^2[/latex]
Area = [latex]1.0 \times 0.5 = 0.5 m^2[/latex]
[latex]F_{water} = 8.75 \times 0.5 = 4.375[/latex] kN

Total force:
[latex]F = F_{oil} + F_{water} = 0.469 + 4.375 = \mathbf{4.84 \text{ kN}}[/latex]

questions.question:
A centrifugal pump is delivering water from an underground tank to an overhead 
reservoir against a static head of 35 m through a 2 km long, 250 mm diameter pipe. 
The head-discharge characteristic of the pump is given by [latex]H = 140 - 9000Q^2[/latex] where [latex]H[/latex] is the head (in m)  generated by the pump and [latex]Q[/latex] is the discharge (in [latex]m^3/s[/latex]) of the pump. Neglecting all minor losses, the head (in m) generated by the pump is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer). Use: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor  [latex]f = 0.04[/latex], Acceleration due to gravity[latex] = 9.81 m/s^2[/latex], [latex]\pi = 3.14[/latex]
questions.explanation: Given: Static head [latex]= 35 m, L = 2000 m, D = 250 mm = 0.25 m, f = 0.04, g = 9.81 m/s^2, \pi= 3.14[/latex] Pump curve: [latex]H = 140 - 9000Q^2[/latex] Step 1  -  Friction head loss (Darcy-Weisbach): [latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{fL}{2gD} \times \dfrac{16Q^2}{\pi^2 D^4}[/latex]... Using: [latex]h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex] [latex]h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000 \times Q^2}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{9.8596 \times 9.81 \times 0.000977}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{0.09444}[/latex][latex]= 6778 Q^2[/latex] Step 2  -  System curve: [latex]H_{sys} = 35 + 6778 Q^2[/latex] Step 3  -  Operating point (pump curve = system curve): [latex]140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6778Q^2[/latex] [latex]105 = 15778 Q^2[/latex] [latex]Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15778} = 0.006655[/latex] [latex]Q = 0.08158 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}[/latex] Step 4  -  Head generated: [latex]H = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006655 = 140 - 59.9 = \mathbf{80 \text{ m}} [/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: Static head [latex]= 35 m, L = 2000 m, D = 250 mm = 0.25 m, f = 0.04, g = 9.81 m/s^2, \pi= 3.14[/latex]
Pump curve: [latex]H = 140 - 9000Q^2[/latex]

Step 1 - Friction head loss (Darcy-Weisbach):
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{fLV^2}{2gD} = \dfrac{fL}{2gD} \times \dfrac{16Q^2}{\pi^2 D^4}[/latex]...

Using: [latex]h_f = \dfrac{8fLQ^2}{\pi^2 g D^5}[/latex]
[latex]h_f = \dfrac{8 \times 0.04 \times 2000 \times Q^2}{(3.14)^2 \times 9.81 \times (0.25)^5}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{9.8596 \times 9.81 \times 0.000977}[/latex][latex]= \dfrac{640 Q^2}{0.09444}[/latex][latex]= 6778 Q^2[/latex]

Step 2 - System curve:
[latex]H_{sys} = 35 + 6778 Q^2[/latex]

Step 3 - Operating point (pump curve = system curve):
[latex]140 - 9000Q^2 = 35 + 6778Q^2[/latex]
[latex]105 = 15778 Q^2[/latex]
[latex]Q^2 = \dfrac{105}{15778} = 0.006655[/latex]
[latex]Q = 0.08158 \text{ m}^3/\text{s}[/latex]

Step 4 - Head generated:
[latex]H = 140 - 9000 \times 0.006655 = 140 - 59.9 = \mathbf{80 \text{ m}} [/latex]

questions.question: The flow depth for a discharge of 10 [latex]m^3/s[/latex] in a wide rectangular channel is 2.0 m. Assume that the flow is uniform. If the discharge is doubled, the flow depth (in m) in this channel is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Manning's equation for a wide rectangular channel: [latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}[/latex] For wide channel: [latex]R \approx y[/latex] (hydraulic radius ≈ depth) [latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}[/latex] So for a wide channel: [latex]Q \propto y^{5/3}[/latex] (when B, n, S are constant) Given: [latex]Q_1 = 10m^3/s[/latex]  at [latex]y_1 = 2.0[/latex] m [latex]Q_2 = 20[/latex] m³/s (doubled) Ratio: [latex]\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3}[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3}[/latex] [latex]2 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2}\right)^{5/3}[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{y_2}{2} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} = 1.5157[/latex] [latex]y_2 = 2 \times 1.5157 = \mathbf{3.03 \text{ m}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Manning's equation for a wide rectangular channel:
[latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times A \times R^{2/3} \times S^{1/2}[/latex]
For wide channel: [latex]R \approx y[/latex] (hydraulic radius ≈ depth)
[latex]Q = \dfrac{1}{n} \times B \times y \times y^{2/3} \times S^{1/2} = \dfrac{B S^{1/2}}{n} \times y^{5/3}[/latex]

So for a wide channel: [latex]Q \propto y^{5/3}[/latex] (when B, n, S are constant)

Given: [latex]Q_1 = 10m^3/s[/latex] at [latex]y_1 = 2.0[/latex] m
[latex]Q_2 = 20[/latex] m³/s (doubled)

Ratio:
[latex]\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{20}{10} = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2.0}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]2 = \left(\dfrac{y_2}{2}\right)^{5/3}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{y_2}{2} = 2^{3/5} = 2^{0.6} = 1.5157[/latex]
[latex]y_2 = 2 \times 1.5157 = \mathbf{3.03 \text{ m}}[/latex]

questions.question: For a clayey soil stratum, the time required for degree of consolidation from 25% to 50% is 30 days. The total time (in days) required for 90% degree of consolidation of the same soil stratum is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Consolidation theory  -  Time factor [latex]T_v[/latex]: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{H^2}[/latex] For a given soil layer, [latex]C_v/H^2[/latex] is constant [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]t \propto T_v[/latex] Time factors for different degrees of consolidation (U): For U = 25%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{25}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.0625 = 0.04909[/latex] For U = 50%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.25 = 0.1963[/latex] For U = 90%: [latex]T_v = 0.848[/latex] (standard value) Ratio [latex]t_{90}/t_{25\to50}[/latex]: Time from 25% to 50% = 30 days corresponds to [latex]\Delta T_v = 0.1963 - 0.04909 = 0.1472[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{C_v}{H^2} = \dfrac{0.1472}{30} = 0.004907 \text{ day}^{-1}[/latex] Time for U = 90%: [latex]t_{90} = \dfrac{0.848}{0.004907} = \mathbf{172.8 \approx 173 \text{ days}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Consolidation theory - Time factor [latex]T_v[/latex]:
[latex]T_v = \dfrac{C_v \cdot t}{H^2}[/latex]

For a given soil layer, [latex]C_v/H^2[/latex] is constant [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]t \propto T_v[/latex]

Time factors for different degrees of consolidation (U):
For U = 25%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{25}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.0625 = 0.04909[/latex]
For U = 50%: [latex]T_v = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \times 0.25 = 0.1963[/latex]
For U = 90%: [latex]T_v = 0.848[/latex] (standard value)

Ratio [latex]t_{90}/t_{25\to50}[/latex]:
Time from 25% to 50% = 30 days corresponds to [latex]\Delta T_v = 0.1963 - 0.04909 = 0.1472[/latex]

[latex]\dfrac{C_v}{H^2} = \dfrac{0.1472}{30} = 0.004907 \text{ day}^{-1}[/latex]

Time for U = 90%:
[latex]t_{90} = \dfrac{0.848}{0.004907} = \mathbf{172.8 \approx 173 \text{ days}}[/latex]

questions.question: The ultimate bearing capacity of a 1 m wide strip footing is 532.80 kPa, when embedded at 1 m depth in dry cohesionless soil. The soil has a unit weight of 18 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The ultimate bearing capacity is 864 kPa when the depth of embedment becomes 2 m. Neglecting the effect of the depth factor, the bearing capacity factor [latex]N_q[/latex] is ______ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: Terzaghi's bearing capacity for strip footing (cohesionless soil, c = 0): [latex]q_u = q N_q + \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gamma[/latex] where [latex]q = \gamma D_f[/latex] (surcharge from overburden) Given: [latex]B = 1 m, y = 18 kN/m^3[/latex] Case 1: [latex]D_f = 1[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_1 = 18 \times 1 = 18 kN/m^2[/latex] [latex]532.80 = 18 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (1)[/latex] Case 2: [latex]D_f = 2[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_2 = 18 \times 2 = 36 kN/m^2[/latex] [latex]864 = 36 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (2)[/latex] Subtracting (1) from (2): [latex]864 - 532.80 = (36 - 18)N_q[/latex] [latex]331.20 = 18 N_q[/latex] [latex]N_q = \dfrac{331.20}{18} = \mathbf{18.4}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Terzaghi's bearing capacity for strip footing (cohesionless soil, c = 0):
[latex]q_u = q N_q + \dfrac{1}{2}\gamma B N_\gamma[/latex]
where [latex]q = \gamma D_f[/latex] (surcharge from overburden)

Given:
[latex]B = 1 m, y = 18 kN/m^3[/latex]

Case 1: [latex]D_f = 1[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_1 = 18 \times 1 = 18 kN/m^2[/latex]
[latex]532.80 = 18 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]

Case 2: [latex]D_f = 2[/latex] m [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]q_2 = 18 \times 2 = 36 kN/m^2[/latex]
[latex]864 = 36 N_q + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 18 \times 1 \times N_\gamma \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Subtracting (1) from (2):
[latex]864 - 532.80 = (36 - 18)N_q[/latex]
[latex]331.20 = 18 N_q[/latex]

questions.question:
A building is proposed in an area having thick deposit of silty clay. The water table 
is at the ground surface. The saturated unit weight of soil is 18 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex] and unit weight of water is 10 [latex]kN/m^3[/latex]. The maximum vertical load ([latex]P[/latex]) on a column of the 
proposed building is 2000 kN. Consider [latex]\sigma_z \leq 0.1\,\sigma'_v[/latex] for computation of minimum depth of soil exploration. [latex]\sigma'_v[/latex] is the effective vertical overburden stress. [latex]\sigma_z [/latex] is the increase in the vertical stress at depth [latex]z[/latex] below load [latex]P[/latex] as per the Boussinesq's stress theory. Based on above, the minimum depth (in m) of soil exploration required for the 
foundation design is ________ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: Water table at ground surface, [latex]\gamma_{sat} = 18kN/m^3, \gamma_w = 10 kN/m^3[/latex] Column load P = 2000 kN Condition: [latex]\sigma_z \leq 0.1 \sigma'_v[/latex] at depth z Step 1  -  Effective vertical stress at depth z (water table at surface): [latex]\sigma'_v = (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) \times z = (18 - 10) \times z = 8zkN/m^2[/latex] Step 2  -  Stress increase below column (Boussinesq, for circular/point load): For a point load P: [latex]\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2}[/latex] (at depth z directly below load) Step 3  -  Apply condition: [latex]\dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.1 \times 8z[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{3 \times 2000}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.8z[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{6000}{2\pi z^2} = 0.8z[/latex] [latex]z^3 = \dfrac{6000}{2\pi \times 0.8} = \dfrac{6000}{5.027} = 1193.7[/latex] [latex]z = (1193.7)^{1/3} = \mathbf{10.61 \text{ m}}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Water table at ground surface, [latex]\gamma_{sat} = 18kN/m^3, \gamma_w = 10 kN/m^3[/latex]
Column load P = 2000 kN
Condition: [latex]\sigma_z \leq 0.1 \sigma'_v[/latex] at depth z

Step 1 - Effective vertical stress at depth z (water table at surface):
[latex]\sigma'_v = (\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w) \times z = (18 - 10) \times z = 8zkN/m^2[/latex]

Step 2 - Stress increase below column (Boussinesq, for circular/point load):
For a point load P: [latex]\sigma_z = \dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2}[/latex] (at depth z directly below load)

Step 3 - Apply condition:
[latex]\dfrac{3P}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.1 \times 8z[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{3 \times 2000}{2\pi z^2} \leq 0.8z[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{6000}{2\pi z^2} = 0.8z[/latex]
[latex]z^3 = \dfrac{6000}{2\pi \times 0.8} = \dfrac{6000}{5.027} = 1193.7[/latex]
[latex]z = (1193.7)^{1/3} = \mathbf{10.61 \text{ m}}[/latex]

Liquidity Index [latex]LI = 50\% = 0.5[/latex]

questions.question: For a given traffic stream, the speed-density relationship is given as: [latex]v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)[/latex] where [latex]v[/latex] is the mean speed (in km/h) and [latex]k[/latex] is the density (in veh/km). Considering [latex]v_o = 45[/latex] km/h and [latex]k_j = 200[/latex] veh/km, the maximum flow (in veh/h) for the given stream is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation: Given speed-density model: [latex]v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)[/latex] where [latex]v_o = 45[/latex] km/h, [latex]k_j = 200[/latex] veh/km Step 1  -  Flow = speed x density: [latex]q = v \cdot k = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) \cdot k[/latex] Step 2  -  Maximize flow [latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0[/latex]: [latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) + k \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)\right] = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) - 1\right] = 0[/latex] [latex]\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{k_j}{k} = e \Rightarrow k^* = \dfrac{k_j}{e} = \dfrac{200}{e} = \dfrac{200}{2.718} = 73.57[/latex] veh/km Step 3  -  Speed at maximum flow: [latex]v^* = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k^*}\right) = 45 \times \ln(e) = 45 \times 1 = 45[/latex] km/h Step 4  -  Maximum flow: [latex]q_{max} = v^* \times k^* = 45 \times 73.57 = \mathbf{3311 \text{ veh/h}}[/latex]

Given speed-density model: [latex]v = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right)[/latex]

where [latex]v_o = 45[/latex] km/h, [latex]k_j = 200[/latex] veh/km

Step 1 - Flow = speed x density:
[latex]q = v \cdot k = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) \cdot k[/latex]

Step 2 - Maximize flow [latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = 0[/latex]:
[latex]\dfrac{dq}{dk} = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) + k \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{k}\right)\right] = v_o\left[\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) - 1\right] = 0[/latex]
[latex]\ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k}\right) = 1 \Rightarrow \dfrac{k_j}{k} = e \Rightarrow k^* = \dfrac{k_j}{e} = \dfrac{200}{e} = \dfrac{200}{2.718} = 73.57[/latex] veh/km

Step 3 - Speed at maximum flow:
[latex]v^* = v_o \ln\left(\dfrac{k_j}{k^*}\right) = 45 \times \ln(e) = 45 \times 1 = 45[/latex] km/h

Step 4 - Maximum flow:
[latex]q_{max} = v^* \times k^* = 45 \times 73.57 = \mathbf{3311 \text{ veh/h}}[/latex]

Consider the following: Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) = 90 m Height of headlight of a vehicle above the road surface = 0.75 m Headlight beam angle with respect to the longitudinal axis of the vehicle = 1.2[latex]^\circ [/latex] Based on the sight distance criteria, the design length (in m) of the vertical curve is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).

Given: Descending gradient:

[latex]
g_1=-\frac{1}{40}=-0.025=-2.5\%
[/latex] Ascending gradient:

[latex]
g_2=\frac{1}{50}=0.02=2.0\%
[/latex] Algebraic difference of grades:
[latex]
N=|g_1-g_2|
=|-2.5-2.0|

(percent) Stopping Sight Distance:

[latex]

[/latex] Headlight beam angle:

[latex]
\phi=1.2^\circ

[latex]
L > S,
[/latex] IRC recommends

[latex]
L=\dfrac{N S^2}{200\left(h+S\tan\phi\right)}
[/latex] Step 2: Calculate the denominator [latex]
\tan(1.2^\circ)\approx 0.02095
[/latex] [latex]
h+S\tan\phi
=
0.75+90(0.02095)
[/latex]

[latex]
=
0.75+1.8855
=
2.6355
[/latex] Thus,

[latex]
200(h+S\tan\phi)
=
200(2.6355)
=
527.1
[/latex] Step 3: Calculate the curve length [latex]
L
=
\frac{4.5\times90^2}{527.1}
[/latex]

[latex]
=
\frac{4.5\times8100}{527.1}
[/latex]

[latex]
=
\frac{36450}{527.1}
[/latex]

[latex]
\approx69.15\ \text{m}

[latex]
L < S
[/latex], 

the assumption is not valid. Therefore, use the IRC equation for

[latex]
L < S:
[/latex] [latex]
L
=
2S-\dfrac{200(h+S\tan\phi)}{N}
[/latex] Substituting values, [latex]
L
=
2(90)-\dfrac{200(2.6355)}{4.5}
[/latex]

[latex]
=
180-117.13
[/latex]

[latex]
=

questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Descending gradient: [latex] g_1=-\frac{1}{40}=-0.025=-2.5\% [/latex]
Ascending gradient: [latex] g_2=\frac{1}{50}=0.02=2.0\% [/latex]
Algebraic difference of grades: [latex] N=|g_1-g_2| =|-2.5-2.0| =4.5 [/latex] (percent)
Stopping Sight Distance: [latex] S=90\ \text{m} [/latex]
Headlight height: [latex] h=0.75\ \text{m} [/latex]
Headlight beam angle: [latex] \phi=1.2^\circ [/latex]
Step 1: Identify the type of vertical curve
A descending gradient meeting an ascending gradient forms a sag vertical curve.
For a sag curve, when sight distance is governed by headlights and [latex] L > S, [/latex]
IRC recommends [latex] L=\dfrac{N S^2}{200\left(h+S\tan\phi\right)} [/latex]
Step 2: Calculate the denominator
[latex] \tan(1.2^\circ)\approx 0.02095 [/latex]
[latex] h+S\tan\phi = 0.75+90(0.02095) [/latex] [latex] = 0.75+1.8855 = 2.6355 [/latex]
Thus, [latex] 200(h+S\tan\phi) = 200(2.6355) = 527.1 [/latex]
Step 3: Calculate the curve length
[latex] L = \frac{4.5\times90^2}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] = \frac{4.5\times8100}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] = \frac{36450}{527.1} [/latex] [latex] \approx69.15\ \text{m} [/latex]

Therefore, use the IRC equation for [latex] L < S: [/latex]
[latex] L = 2S-\dfrac{200(h+S\tan\phi)}{N} [/latex]
Substituting values,
[latex] L = 2(90)-\dfrac{200(2.6355)}{4.5} [/latex] [latex] = 180-117.13 [/latex] [latex] = 62.87\ \text{m} [/latex]
Rounded to the nearest integer, [latex] \boxed{63\ \text{m}} [/latex]

questions.question: In an industry, a cyclone collector with 80% efficiency is installed for air purification, followed by an electrostatic precipitator with 50% efficiency. The concentration of particles entering the cyclone collector is 10 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]. The concentration (in [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]) of particles exiting the precipitator is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Given: Inlet concentration = 10 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Cyclone efficiency = 80% ESP efficiency = 50% Step 1  -  After cyclone collector: Particles removed = 80% of 10 = 8 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Particles exiting cyclone = 10 − 8 = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Step 2  -  After electrostatic precipitator (ESP): Particles entering ESP = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Particles removed by ESP = 50% of 2 = 1 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Particles exiting ESP = 2 − 1 = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex] Final concentration exiting the precipitator = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given:
Inlet concentration = 10 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Cyclone efficiency = 80%
ESP efficiency = 50%

Step 1 - After cyclone collector:
Particles removed = 80% of 10 = 8 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles exiting cyclone = 10 − 8 = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

Step 2 - After electrostatic precipitator (ESP):
Particles entering ESP = 2 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles removed by ESP = 50% of 2 = 1 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]
Particles exiting ESP = 2 − 1 = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

Final concentration exiting the precipitator = 1.00 [latex]mg/m^3[/latex]

questions.question: If a positive real [latex]x[/latex] satisfies the following equation [latex]\log_2 x + \log_{\sqrt{2}} x = 48[/latex] then the value of [latex]x[/latex] is ________________.
questions.explanation: Given: [latex]\log_2 x + \log_{\sqrt{2}} x = 48[/latex] Step 1  -  Convert [latex]\log_{\sqrt{2}} x[/latex] to base 2: [latex]\log_{\sqrt{2}} x = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{\log_2 \sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\log_2 x}{1/2} = 2\log_2 x[/latex] Step 2  -  Substitute: [latex]\log_2 x + 2\log_2 x = 48[/latex] [latex]3\log_2 x = 48[/latex] [latex]\log_2 x = 16[/latex] Step 3  -  Solve for x: [latex]x = 2^{16}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]\log_2 x + \log_{\sqrt{2}} x = 48[/latex]

Step 1 - Convert [latex]\log_{\sqrt{2}} x[/latex] to base 2:

questions.question: The next figure (indicated by '?') in the sequence is:
'All the mangoes in the basket are good.' If the above statement is false , then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?

options.A: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.
options.B: No mango in the basket is good.
options.C: In the basket some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.
options.D: There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.

questions.explanation: Logic analysis using negation of universal quantifier: The original statement is: 'All mangoes are good' [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] In logic: [latex]\forall x: G(x)[/latex] The negation of a universal statement [latex]\forall x: P(x)[/latex] is the existential statement [latex]\exists x: \neg P(x)[/latex]. So if 'All mangoes are good' is FALSE , then: [latex]\exists x: \neg G(x)[/latex] = 'There exists at least one mango that is NOT good' Why other options are wrong: (A) 'All mangoes are not good' = None are good  -  too strong, not necessarily true (B) 'No mango is good'  -  same as (A), too extreme (C) 'Some good and some not good'  -  possible but not necessarily true (could be all bad) Only (D) is the logical negation that is necessarily true.
questions.explanation_html:
Logic analysis using negation of universal quantifier:

The original statement is: 'All mangoes are good' [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] In logic: [latex]\forall x: G(x)[/latex]

The negation of a universal statement [latex]\forall x: P(x)[/latex] is the existential statement [latex]\exists x: \neg P(x)[/latex].

So if 'All mangoes are good' is FALSE, then:
[latex]\exists x: \neg G(x)[/latex] = 'There exists at least one mango that is NOT good'

Why other options are wrong:
(A) 'All mangoes are not good' = None are good - too strong, not necessarily true
(B) 'No mango is good' - same as (A), too extreme
(C) 'Some good and some not good' - possible but not necessarily true (could be all bad)

Only (D) is the logical negation that is necessarily true.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about four numbers: (S1) The average of the four numbers is 25 (S2) Each number is at most 40 (S3) Each number is at least 20 Choose the option that is necessarily correct.
questions.explanation: Testing each option: Option (A): S1 + S2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3? S1: average = 25, S2: each ≤ 40. Can a number be < 20? Yes  -  e.g., {5, 30, 30, 35}: avg = 25, all ≤ 40, but 5 < 20. So S3 is NOT guaranteed. Option (B): S2 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S1? S2: each ≤ 40, S3: each ≥ 20. Average could be anything between 20 and 40. Not necessarily 25. Option (C): S1 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S2? S1: average = 25, so sum = 100. S3: each ≥ 20. If one number > 40, say [latex]a > 40[/latex], then [latex]a + b + c + d = 100[/latex] with [latex]b, c, d \geq 20[/latex]. So [latex]b + c + d \geq 60[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]a \leq 40[/latex]. Contradiction! Therefore no number can exceed 40. Option (D): S1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3? Average = 25 doesn't mean each ≥ 20 (e.g., {5, 25, 35, 35}). Therefore, (C) is necessarily correct .
questions.explanation_html:
Testing each option:

Option (A): S1 + S2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3?
S1: average = 25, S2: each ≤ 40. Can a number be < 20? Yes - e.g., {5, 30, 30, 35}: avg = 25, all ≤ 40, but 5 < 20. So S3 is NOT guaranteed.

Option (B): S2 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S1?
S2: each ≤ 40, S3: each ≥ 20. Average could be anything between 20 and 40. Not necessarily 25.

Option (C): S1 + S3 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S2?
S1: average = 25, so sum = 100. S3: each ≥ 20.
If one number > 40, say [latex]a > 40[/latex], then [latex]a + b + c + d = 100[/latex] with [latex]b, c, d \geq 20[/latex].
So [latex]b + c + d \geq 60[/latex] [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] [latex]a \leq 40[/latex]. Contradiction! Therefore no number can exceed 40.

Option (D): S1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] S3?
Average = 25 doesn't mean each ≥ 20 (e.g., {5, 25, 35, 35}).

Therefore, (C) is necessarily correct.

questions.question:
The table lists the unit selling price of five products P, Q, R, S, and T. On a particular day, 250 items were sold with the average selling price of Rs. 60. The following observations were made: (i) The quantity of S sold was twice that of T. (ii) The quantity of R sold was thrice that of T. (iii) The quantity of Q sold was four times that of T. [latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline \text{Product} & P & Q & R & S & T \\
\hline \text{Unit selling price (Rs.)} & 100 & 50 & 40 & 60 & 60 \\
\hline
\end{array}[/latex] What is the quantity of product P sold on that day?
questions.explanation: Let quantity of T = t Then: S = 2t, R = 3t, Q = 4t Step 1  -  Total quantity equation: [latex]P + Q + R + S + T = 250[/latex] [latex]P + 4t + 3t + 2t + t = 250[/latex] [latex]P + 10t = 250 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex] Step 2  -  Total revenue equation: Average price = Rs. 60, Total items = 250 Total revenue = [latex]250 \times 60 = 15000[/latex] Rs. [latex]100P + 50(4t) + 40(3t) + 60(2t) + 60t = 15000[/latex] [latex]100P + 200t + 120t + 120t + 60t = 15000[/latex] [latex]100P + 500t = 15000[/latex] [latex]P + 5t = 150 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex] Step 3  -  Subtract (2) from (1): [latex](P + 10t) - (P + 5t) = 250 - 150[/latex] [latex]5t = 100 \Rightarrow t = 20[/latex] Step 4  -  Find P: [latex]P = 250 - 10(20) = 250 - 200 = \mathbf{50}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Let quantity of T = t
Then: S = 2t, R = 3t, Q = 4t

Step 1 - Total quantity equation:
[latex]P + Q + R + S + T = 250[/latex]
[latex]P + 4t + 3t + 2t + t = 250[/latex]
[latex]P + 10t = 250 \quad \cdots (1)[/latex]

Step 2 - Total revenue equation:
Average price = Rs. 60, Total items = 250
Total revenue = [latex]250 \times 60 = 15000[/latex] Rs.

[latex]100P + 50(4t) + 40(3t) + 60(2t) + 60t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]100P + 200t + 120t + 120t + 60t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]100P + 500t = 15000[/latex]
[latex]P + 5t = 150 \quad \cdots (2)[/latex]

Step 3 - Subtract (2) from (1):
[latex](P + 10t) - (P + 5t) = 250 - 150[/latex]
[latex]5t = 100 \Rightarrow t = 20[/latex]

Step 4 - Find P:
[latex]P = 250 - 10(20) = 250 - 200 = \mathbf{50}[/latex]

questions.question: Consider a string P of length [latex]l[/latex] that is laid out as a straight-line segment. Another string K is laid out as a semicircular arc with string P as its diameter as represented in Figure (i). When both strings are shortened by a length [latex]x[/latex], they can be re-arranged such that the shortened string K forms a full circle with the shortened string P as its diameter, as represented in Figure (ii). The value of [latex]\dfrac{x}{l}[/latex] is __________.
questions.explanation: Setup: String P (diameter) has original length [latex]l[/latex]. String K (semicircle) has original length [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex] (semicircle of diameter [latex]l[/latex]). After shortening by x: New P length = [latex]l - x[/latex] (this is now the diameter of the full circle) New K length = [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x[/latex] (this now forms a full circle) Condition  -  K forms a full circle with P as diameter: Circumference of full circle = [latex]\pi \times \text{diameter} = \pi(l - x)[/latex] Setting equal to new K length: [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi(l - x)[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi l - \pi x[/latex] [latex]\pi x - x = \pi l - \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex] [latex]x(\pi - 1) = \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex] [latex]\dfrac{x}{l} = \dfrac{\pi}{2(\pi - 1)}[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
Setup:
String P (diameter) has original length [latex]l[/latex].
String K (semicircle) has original length [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex] (semicircle of diameter [latex]l[/latex]).

After shortening by x:
New P length = [latex]l - x[/latex] (this is now the diameter of the full circle)
New K length = [latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x[/latex] (this now forms a full circle)

Condition - K forms a full circle with P as diameter:
Circumference of full circle = [latex]\pi \times \text{diameter} = \pi(l - x)[/latex]

Setting equal to new K length:
[latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi(l - x)[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{\pi l}{2} - x = \pi l - \pi x[/latex]
[latex]\pi x - x = \pi l - \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex]
[latex]x(\pi - 1) = \dfrac{\pi l}{2}[/latex]
[latex]\dfrac{x}{l} = \dfrac{\pi}{2(\pi - 1)}[/latex]

questions.question: The Roman senator Meritorius, his brother, his son, and his daughter have varying oratory skill levels. They are seated in rows and columns as shown in the figure with exactly one person sitting in each box. It is known that: (i) Meritorius' daughter and his brother are seated in the same column. (ii) His son is seated diagonally across the sibling of the worst orator. (iii) The best and worst orators are seated in the same row. Who is the best orator?

The siblings in this group are: Br is sibling of M; D is sibling of S... wait  -  Br and M are siblings (brothers). D and S are children of M (so siblings to each other). Worst orator's sibling: if worst = D, sibling = S; if worst = Br, sibling = M. Clue (iii): Best and worst orators are in the same row. Working through: From clue (i): Let D = Row1-C1, Br = Row2-C1 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] M and S fill Row1-C2 and Row2-C2. From clue (ii): Son is diagonal from worst's sibling. If Son = Row2-C2, diagonal = Row1-C1 = D. D is sibling of Son [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] worst orator = Son? But Son can't be diagonal from his own sibling to himself. Try Son = Row1-C2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] diagonal = Row2-C1 = Br. Br is sibling of M [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] worst orator = M. From clue (iii): Best and worst (M) in same row. M = Row2-C2. So best is also in Row 2 [latex] \rightarrow [/latex] best = Br or M. Since M = worst, best = Meritorius' brother
